prompt: Nurse Practitioner Mark S. Brezina(Hematology): A 60-year-old man was seen in the outpatient cancer center at this hospital because of bone pain and skeletal lesions on imaging. The patient had been well until approximately 2 months before this evaluation, when he had a gradual onset of pain in the back of his neck and shoulders, which was followed later by a sharp pain in the middle of his back that began suddenly after sneezing. The pain increased after exercise and did not decrease with physical therapy, massage therapy, or a course of prednisone. One month before this evaluation, computed tomography (CT) of the chest that was performed at another hospital revealed numerous lytic lesions in the thoracic spine and pathologic compression fractures of T5 and T7 (Figure 1). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbar spine with short-tau inversion recovery (STIR) parameters (also performed at the other hospital at that time) revealed numerous lesions with high signal intensity involving the vertebral bodies and posterior elements (Figure 2). CT Scans of the Thoracic Spine.On a sagittal reformatted image obtained 9 months before the initial presentation (Panel A), no lytic lesions are present. On an image obtained 1 month before presentation (Panel B), there are numerous lytic lesions at T5, T6, and T11 (arrows); a lytic lesion at T7 has resulted in a pathologic compression fracture and an approximately 50% loss of height (asterisk). On an image obtained 1 week before presentation (Panel C), there is an increase in the size and number of lytic lesions (arrows), progression of a previously minimal pathologic compression fracture of T5 (arrowhead), and evidence of vertebral augmentation at T7 (asterisk). MRI Scans of the Lumbar Spine.A sagittal image obtained with short-tau inversion recovery (STIR) parameters 1 month before presentation (Panel A) shows numerous lesions with high signal intensity throughout the vertebral bodies and posterior elements of the lumbar spine (arrows). An image obtained with STIR parameters 2 months after the diagnosis (Panel B) shows an increase in the size and number of lesions with high signal intensity (arrows). A lesion at L1 has resulted in a pathologic compression fracture, with approximately 50% loss of height (asterisk). Nurse Practitioner Brezina:Pathological examination of a bone marrow–biopsy specimen that was obtained at that time reportedly revealed mildly hypocellular bone marrow with maturing trilineage hematopoiesis. Immunoperoxidase stains for CD34, CD117, CD3, CD20, and CD138 and in situ hybridization for kappa and lambda light chains showed no abnormal cells. Examination of the bone marrow aspirate revealed maturing trilineage hematopoiesis and scattered mast cells, including occasional cells with an atypical spindle-shaped appearance. Flow cytometric and cytogenetic analysis showed a normal male karyotype; fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) testing for aCHIC2deletion associated withFIP1L1–PDGFRAfusion was negative. A narcotic analgesic agent was administered. The level of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) was 2.9 ng per milliliter. One week later, a CT-guided biopsy of a lesion in the iliac crest was performed, and examination of the specimen reportedly revealed slightly hypocellular marrow and a mildly increased number of CD117+ mast cells, including spindle-shaped cells. A kyphoplasty procedure was performed at T7 for pain relief; pathological examination of a biopsy specimen of the T7 vertebra reportedly revealed necrosis, fibrosis, and bone remodeling, with prominent osteoclastic activity. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed a few CD117+ mast cells in fibrotic marrow, with no definite coexpression of CD2 or CD25 cells. Ghosts of spindle-shaped cells were observed in necrotic areas. The hematocrit was 37.8% (reference range, 41.0 to 53.0), the erythrocyte sedimentation rate 74 mm per hour (reference range, 0 to 15), and the blood level of tryptase 20 ng per milliliter (reference range, 2 to 10). The white-cell count and differential count were normal, as were blood levels of electrolytes and β2-microglobulin, results of liver-function tests and serum protein electrophoresis, and the 24-hour urinary histamine level. Testing for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus types 1 and 2 was reportedly negative, as was FISH analysis for theBCR-ABLrearrangement and testing of peripheral-blood leukocytes for the Janus kinase 2 (JAK2) V617F mutation and theKITD816V mutation. Nine days before the current evaluation,18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron-emission tomography and CT (PET–CT) revealed FDG-avid lesions throughout the axial and appendicular skeleton (Figure 3). Combination18F-Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) Positron-Emission Tomography and CT (PET–CT) Scans.On axial PET–CT images, there are FDG-avid lesions in numerous bones, including the cervical spine (Panel A, arrow), sternum and right scapula (Panel B, arrows), thoracic spine and left eighth rib (Panel C, arrows), upper lumbar spine (Panel D, arrows), lower lumbar spine and iliac bones (Panel E, arrows), and right ischium and right femoral head (Panel F, arrows). Nurse Practitioner Brezina:The day before this evaluation, the patient was seen in the allergy and immunology clinic at a second hospital. Physical examination revealed no cutaneous urticaria, urticaria pigmentosa, or angioedema. Review of the bone marrow aspirate and biopsy specimens and the iliac bone and vertebral-body biopsy specimens showed features that were interpreted as suspicious for but not diagnostic of systemic mastocytosis; repeat biopsy of a bone lesion and the administration of interferon-α were recommended. The next day, the patient was seen in the cancer center at this hospital. The patient reported severe pain in the neck, back, and pelvic bone, as well as decreased appetite and a weight loss of 4.5 kg during the previous 2 months, intermittent mild heartburn, and no flushing, tachycardia, pruritus, urticaria pigmentosa, or diarrhea. Urinary retention had developed after initiation of pain medications, and he reported psychological stress and anxiety. He had a history of shingles, and until 5 years before this illness, he had had occasional episodes of syncope when standing. There was no history of gastric ulcers, bone fractures, abnormal blood counts, allergic rhinitis, heart disease, or prior surgeries. Medications included alprazolam, mirtazapine, zoledronic acid (administered once by infusion 1 week earlier), a fentanyl patch, hydromorphone, and tamsulosin (for urinary retention after the administration of pain medication). He had no known allergies. He was married and worked at a health care organization. He had a smoking history of 40 pack-years, currently smoked a half pack of cigarettes per day, and drank alcohol occasionally. His mother was over 90 years of age and had dementia, and his father had died at 84 years of age with coronary artery disease and prostate cancer; there was no family history of hematologic cancers. On examination, the patient was alert, oriented, and in pain. The vital signs and oxygen saturation were normal. There was mild midepigastric tenderness on deep palpation, without rebound, and tenderness on palpation of the spine in the mid-thoracic and lumbosacral regions. The remainder of the examination was normal. The hematocrit was 37.8%, the blood level of lactate dehydrogenase 251 U per liter (reference range, 110 to 210), the globulin level 4.4 g per deciliter (reference range, 2.3 to 4.1), the uric acid level 3.4 mg per deciliter (202 μmol per liter; reference range, 3.6 to 8.5 mg per deciliter [214 to 506 μmol per liter]), and the tryptase level 23.2 ng per milliliter (reference value, <11.5); the platelet count, red-cell indexes, and results of renal- and liver-function tests were normal, as were blood levels of electrolytes, glucose, total protein, albumin, and parathyroid hormone. Urinalysis revealed 1+ ketones and trace occult blood. A diagnostic procedure was performed.

Looking at the imaging results: CT scans showed lytic lesions in the thoracic spine and compression fractures at T5 and T7.

prompt: During an employment health check at Infosys, Bangalore, a 45-year-old man, Narayan, is noted to have a 3 cm palpable nodule in one lobe of an otherwise normal sized thyroid gland. sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this case.

The size of the nodule, 3 cm, isn't too large, but it's definitely something that needs attention.
The needle aspiration results are key here.
Polygonal tumor cells suggest that the cells are arranged in a polygonal pattern, which is a characteristic of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC).
PTC is the most common type of thyroid cancer and is known for its papillary structure with these polygonal cells.
The presence of amyloid in the aspiration is another clue.
Amyloid is a proteinaceous material that can be seen in certain thyroid conditions.
In the context of thyroid nodules, especially those that are solid, the presence of amyloid is often associated with a diagnosis of papillary thyroid carcinoma.
It's a feature that's seen in about 10-15% of PTC cases.
Scanty colloid and normal follicular cells are also noted.
Colloid is a component of the thyroid that's usually seen in benign conditions like colloid goiter or nodules.
The fact that it's scanty might indicate that the nodule isn't a simple cyst or a benign nodule, supporting the idea that it's a more aggressive or malignant process.
I should also consider other possibilities.

For example, medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) is another type of thyroid cancer, but it's usually associated with multiple nodules, calcifications, and is often linked to MENA or MENA-like syndromes.
The presentation here doesn't mention multiple nodules or calcifications, so MTC is less likely.
Another consideration is a follicular thyroid neoplasm, which is a type of thyroid cancer that can present as a solid nodule.
However, follicular neoplasms typically have a more infiltrative growth pattern and may not show the polygonal cells as clearly as PTC does.
Additionally, the presence of amyloid is not a common feature of follicular neoplasms, making PTC a stronger possibility.

Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune condition that can cause thyroid enlargement, but it's usually associated with diffuse goiter and is less likely to present as a single nodule with these aspiration findings.
So, putting it all together: the nodule is solid, the aspiration shows polygonal cells (indicative of PTC), and there's amyloid present.
These are strong indicators for papillary thyroid carcinoma.
The scanty colloid further supports this, as it's not a typical feature of PTC but aligns with the idea that the nodule is more concerning for malignancy.
I should also think about the patient's age.
He's 45, which is within the range where thyroid cancer can occur, though more commonly in older adults.
However, PTC can occur at any age, including in younger individuals.

In terms of treatment, if this is confirmed as PTC, the next steps would likely involve a thyroidectomy to remove the nodule and possibly some surrounding tissue to ensure no microscopic cancer cells remain.
Lymph node evaluation might also be necessary to check for metastasis.
So, after considering all these points, the most likely diagnosis is papillary thyroid carcinoma.
The patient's thyroid nodule presentation with polygonal tumor cells, amyloid, and scanty colloid points towards papillary thyroid carcinoma.

prompt: A 53-year-old man was admitted to this hospital because of shock and recurrent ventricular tachycardia after defibrillator placement for nonischemic cardiomyopathy. The patient had been in his usual state of health until 4 weeks before this admission, when he was on vacation in the Caribbean and his wife noted that he was unresponsive, “gurgling,” and diaphoretic in the early morning. When he awoke, he reported chest pain, palpitations, and light-headedness. The patient was taken by ambulance to a local hospital, where the heart rate was 65 beats per minute, the blood pressure 100/56 mm Hg, and the oxygen saturation 100% while he was breathing oxygen through a nasal cannula at a rate of 2 liters per minute. The troponin T level was 1.56 ng per milliliter (normal range, <0.01), and the lactate level was 1.9 mmol per liter (17 mg per deciliter; normal range, 0.5 to 1.6 mmol per liter [5 to 14 mg per deciliter]). A complete blood count and levels of electrolytes, magnesium, calcium, and amylase were normal, as were results of tests of renal and thyroid function; ad-dimer level was undetectable. While the patient was in the local hospital, monomorphic ventricular tachycardia developed at a heart rate of 201 beats per minute; electrocardioversion resulted in restoration of sinus rhythm. Aspirin, clopidogrel, enoxaparin, rosuvastatin, amiodarone, and tirofiban were administered. The patient was transferred by air to a hospital in Florida. On examination at the second hospital, the temperature was 36.8°C, the heart rate 57 beats per minute, the blood pressure 122/90 mm Hg, the respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and the oxygen saturation 99% while the patient was breathing oxygen through a nasal cannula at a rate of 2 liters per minute. The remainder of the examination was normal. The blood troponin I level was 116.00 ng per milliliter (normal range, ≤0.05). A complete blood count, results of renal-function tests, levels of electrolytes and thyrotropin, and the prothrombin and partial-thromboplastin times were normal. An electrocardiogram (Figure 1A) showed sinus bradycardia, a ventricular ectopic beat, first-degree atrioventricular delay, and delayed intraventricular conduction. Aspirin, amiodarone, enoxaparin, and atorvastatin were administered. Ventricular tachycardia recurred at a heart rate of 176 beats per minute. Despite the administration of an intravenous bolus of amiodarone, ventricular tachycardia persisted. Electrocardioversion restored sinus rhythm. The patient was admitted to the hospital, and cardiac studies were performed. Initial Cardiac Studies, Obtained at the Second Hospital.Cardiac studies were obtained during the patient’s initial hospitalization in Florida. An electrocardiogram (Panel A) shows sinus bradycardia, a ventricular ectopic beat, borderline first-degree atrioventricular delay, delayed intraventricular conduction, and a normal frontal-plane QRS axis. A transthoracic echocardiogram obtained in a parasternal long-axis view (Panel B) shows mildly increased thickness of the interventricular septum (measuring 13 mm) and a mildly dilated left ventricle (measuring 60 mm at end diastole). Cardiac MRI was also performed. A fat-suppressed, T2-weighted image obtained in a short-axis view (Panel C) shows a hyperintense septum (arrows), a finding consistent with myocardial edema. An image with late gadolinium enhancement, obtained in a short-axis view (Panel D), shows patchy enhancement in the septum at the subepicardial location, with extension into the subendocardial layer of the midanterior segment; subepicardial gadolinium enhancement is also seen in the inferolateral wall of the left ventricle (arrows). An image with late gadolinium enhancement, obtained in a four-chamber view (Panel E), shows nodular foci in the midwall of the septum, as well as subepicardial gadolinium enhancement in the inferolateral wall of the left ventricle (arrows). Coronary angiography revealed no evidence of obstructive coronary disease. On ventriculography, the left ventricle was mildly and diffusely hypokinetic, and the left ventricular end-diastolic pressure was 22 mm Hg (normal range, 8 to 15). Transthoracic echocardiography (Figure 1B) revealed a dilated left ventricle with an end-diastolic dimension of 60 mm (normal range, 42 to 58) and an ejection fraction of 35% (normal range, 55 to 70); there was diffuse hypokinesis that was most notable in the inferior and septal territories, mildly increased wall thickness, and mild mitral regurgitation (seeVideo 1, available with the full text of this article at NEJM.org). Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed the septal hypokinesis and revealed moderate left ventricular dilatation with an ejection fraction of 43%, as well as mild right ventricular dilatation with an ejection fraction of 36% (seeVideos 2 and 3, available at NEJM.org). The left ventricular myocardium was normal in thickness. T2-weighted images (Figure 1C) showed marked myocardial edema that was most prominent in the interventricular septum. The ratio of signal in the myocardium to signal in the skeletal muscle was elevated, at 2.4 (normal range, ≤1.9), a finding compatible with edema. Images with late gadolinium enhancement (Figure 1D and 1E) showed patchy, nodular foci in the midwall and subepicardium of the septum and in the inferolateral wall of the left ventricle, with minimal extension into the subendocardium of the anterior segment at the midventricular level. The myocardial edema and pattern of late gadolinium enhancement fulfilled the Lake Louise criteria for the diagnosis of acute myocarditis.1,2 Additional laboratory test results included negative nucleic acid amplification tests of the blood for DNA of adenovirus,Chlamydophila pneumoniae, cytomegalovirus, enterovirus, andMycoplasma pneumoniae, as well as negative nucleic acid amplification tests of a nasopharyngeal swab for DNA ofBordetella pertussis, coronavirus, influenza, parainfluenza, metapneumovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, and rhinovirus. In addition, serologic testing was negative for antibodies to coxsackievirus, human immunodeficiency virus types 1 and 2, Lyme disease, andTrypanosoma cruzi, as well as for IgM antibodies to cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus viral capsid antigen, and parvovirus. Aspirin, metoprolol succinate, and amiodarone were prescribed, and the patient was discharged with a wearable defibrillator vest after a follow-up visit had been scheduled at this hospital. Ten days before this admission, the patient had consultations at this hospital with a cardiologist specializing in the management of heart failure and an electrophysiologist. Vital signs were notable for a heart rate of 49 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 108/70 mm Hg; the examination was otherwise normal. An electrocardiogram (Figure 2A) showed sinus bradycardia and first-degree atrioventricular delay, as well as right bundle-branch block and a left anterior fascicular block (which together constitute bifascicular block). Aspirin was stopped, spironolactone was added, and placement of an implantable cardioverter–defibrillator (ICD) was scheduled. Subsequent Cardiac Studies, Obtained at This Hospital.An electrocardiogram obtained during the patient’s visit to an outpatient clinic at this hospital, 10 days before admission (Panel A), shows sinus bradycardia, first-degree atrioventricular delay, and progression to right bundle-branch block and left anterior fascicular block (which together constitute bifascicular block). A follow-up electrocardiogram obtained shortly after implantation of the implantable cardioverter–defibrillator (ICD) at this hospital (Panel B) shows monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with an extremely wide QRS complex. A transthoracic echocardiogram obtained in a parasternal long-axis view shortly after the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit of this hospital (Panel C) shows thinning of the interventricular septum (arrow), which had decreased in thickness from 13 mm to 7 mm during the 4-week period since the initial echocardiogram had been obtained. On the morning of this admission, during placement of a dual-chamber ICD, episodes of ventricular tachycardia with varying foci were induced. These episodes were terminated with overdrive pacing. After the procedure, ventricular tachycardia developed, with a heart rate of 108 beats per minute (Figure 2B). The blood pressure was 88/53 mm Hg, and a lidocaine infusion was administered. Laboratory test results are shown inTable 1. During the next 10 hours, multiple additional episodes of monomorphic ventricular rhythms occurred, with the heart rate ranging from 90 to 140 beats per minute. The rate of lidocaine infusion was increased, and amiodarone was administered. Early in the morning of the second hospital day, ventricular tachycardia recurred, with associated dyspnea and a blood pressure of 66/40 mm Hg. Normal saline and norepinephrine were administered intravenously. Chest radiography revealed ICD leads in the appropriate position, and bedside echocardiography revealed no evidence of pericardial effusion. The ventricular tachycardia was terminated with antitachycardic pacing, and the ICD was reprogrammed to provide atrial pacing at a rate of 110 beats per minute. The patient was admitted to the cardiac intensive care unit (ICU). Medical history includes no psychiatric conditions. Physical examination shows no abnormalities, and results of laboratory studies are within normal limits.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 37-year-old man.
Let's break down the information given.
He had a sudden financial loss, which led to a bout of illness.
During this time, he felt sad, nervous, and fearful.
He couldn't sleep or eat properly.
Plus, he started hearing voices telling him he was useless and should kill himself.
These symptoms stopped after about a week.
His medical history shows no prior psychiatric issues, and all physical exams and labs are normal.
Hmm, the key points here are the sudden financial stress leading to mental symptoms.
The symptoms included sadness, anxiety, inability to sleep or eat, and auditory hallucinations.
The fact that he's never had similar episodes before makes me think it's a one-time event, not a chronic condition.
Financial loss can definitely cause significant stress, which can sometimes lead to more serious mental health issues.
The hallucinations are a red flag for a possible psychotic disorder.
Since there's no prior history, it's less likely to be a chronic condition like schizophrenia, which often has a gradual onset and a history of similar episodes.
Given that the symptoms resolved after a week, it might be a stress-related episode rather than something more chronic.
Stress can sometimes cause delusional thoughts or hallucinations, which can be a sign of a brief psychotic disorder.
These are often triggered by external stressors like financial problems and can resolve on their own without formal diagnosis.
So, putting it all together, the most likely diagnosis here is Acute Stress-Related Psychosis or Brief Psychotic Disorder, triggered by the financial loss.
It fits the presentation of sudden onset, short duration, and no prior history of mental health issues.
The patient experienced a sudden onset of symptoms following a financial loss, including sadness, anxiety, inability to sleep or eat, and auditory hallucinations.
These resolved within a week without prior psychiatric history, pointing to a stress-related episode rather than a chronic condition.
The most likely diagnosis is Acute Stress-Related Psychosis.

prompt: A 27-yrs-old woman has been feeling low for the past 2 weeks. She has little energy and has trouble concentrating. She states that 6 weeks ago she had been feeling very good, with lots of energy and no need for sleep. She states this pattern has been occurring for at least the past 3 years, though the episodes have never been so severe that she couldn't work.

Okay, so I'm trying to figure out what's going on with this 27-year-old woman.
She's been feeling low for about two weeks now, has low energy, and is having trouble concentrating.
Six weeks ago, she was feeling great with lots of energy and didn't need much sleep.
This pattern has been happening for at least three years, but she's never had it so bad that she couldn't work.
Hmm, let's break this down.
She's experiencing periods of feeling good with lots of energy, followed by periods where she feels low and has trouble concentrating.
This pattern has been recurring for three years.
It doesn't sound like she's having severe episodes that would prevent her from working, which is important.
I remember that some mood disorders have fluctuating symptoms.
Bipolar disorder comes to mind because it involves manic and depressive episodes.
She described a switch from feeling good to feeling low, which fits with the concept of mania or hypomania in bipolar disorder.
The fact that her episodes aren't severe enough to prevent her from working suggests it's a milder form, maybe a type 2 or cyclothymic disorder.
Wait, cyclothymic disorder is a type of bipolar disorder where there are milder mood swings.
It's characterized by periods of hypomania and periods of depression, but the hypomanic episodes aren't as severe as in classical bipolar mania.
Her history of three years with these fluctuations supports this.
Also, the fact that she's had this pattern for a while without the severe episodes points towards a chronic condition like cyclothymic disorder rather than something acute like major depression.
I should also consider other possibilities.
Could it be seasonal affective disorder?
But she's been feeling this way for three years, not just during specific seasons.
Or maybe adjustment disorder?
But she's been feeling this way for so long, and it's recurring, which makes me lean away from that.
Another thought: could it be something like ADHD?
But ADHD usually presents with inattention and hyperactivity, not necessarily mood swings.
Plus, her symptoms are more about low energy and concentration issues, which can be related to mood disorders.
So, putting it all together, the most likely diagnosis is cyclothymic disorder.
It fits her description of fluctuating between good and low energy periods, the duration of the pattern, and the fact that she can still manage her responsibilities.

prompt: A 39-year-old woman presented to this hospital with fever, flank pain, and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Three weeks before admission, the patient was evaluated by her primary care physician. On examination, the temperature was 36.6°C, and she appeared well. There was costovertebral and abdominal tenderness on the right side, without rebound or guarding. The external genitalia were normal. Vaginal metronidazole gel was prescribed. Two days later, the urine culture grew more than 100,000 colony-forming units (CFU) ofEscherichia coliper milliliter and 10,000 to 100,000 CFU ofKlebsiella pneumoniaeper milliliter. A 14-day course of trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole was prescribed. The inguinal swelling reportedly abated, but the flank pain and nausea persisted. Two days after the patient completed the prescribed course of trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, fever and night sweats developed. After 3 days of fever with a temperature of up to 38.5°C, she began vomiting and subsequently presented to the emergency department of this hospital for evaluation. In the emergency department, the patient reported ongoing flank pain, malaise, nausea, and poor appetite with weight loss of 2.3 kg during the past month. There was no sore throat, cough, or diarrhea. She had a history of hypothyroidism, asthma, bipolar disorder, dysmenorrhea, and migraines. She had had multiple urinary tract infections; pyelonephritis had been diagnosed 4 years before this presentation. A copper intrauterine device had been inserted 6 months before this presentation. Medications included albuterol, budesonide–formoterol, divalproex, levothyroxine, loratadine, and sumatriptan as needed for migraines. The patient did not smoke tobacco, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. She had immigrated to the United States from Brazil 1 year earlier; she had been living in New England during the past year and had been working in a laboratory. She had recently spent 3 months in Brazil visiting her husband and had returned to New England shortly before she noted inguinal swelling. While in Brazil, she had remained in a large city and had not visited any remote locations. In New England, she lived alone with one kitten and one full-grown cat. There was no family history of cancer. An aunt had died from tuberculosis, but the patient had had only minimal contact with her aunt. On examination, the temperature was 36.6°C, the blood pressure 100/63 mm Hg, the heart rate 77 beats per minute, the respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and the oxygen saturation 100% while the patient was breathing ambient air. The weight was 67.5 kg and the body-mass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) 24.4. The patient appeared ill. The right side of the abdomen was tender on palpation, without rebound or guarding. Hepatosplenomegaly was not present. Tender bilateral inguinal lymph nodes were noted. No palpable cervical, supraclavicular, infraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy was noted. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. A urine test for human chorionic gonadotropin was negative. Blood levels of glucose, electrolytes, creatine kinase, and lactate dehydrogenase were normal, as were the results of liver-function and kidney-function tests. prompt: A 20-year-old boy came with complaints of sudden pain in the left eye with loss of vision. On examination, left eye cornea was hazy and on looking down, there was a bulging in the lower eyelid.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 20-year-old boy who presented with sudden left eye pain and loss of vision.
The physical exam shows a hazy left cornea and a bulging lower eyelid when looking down.
Let me break this down step by step.
First, the main symptoms here are sudden pain and vision loss in the left eye.
That makes me think of conditions that cause sudden visual issues.
The hazy cornea could indicate an opacity, which might be something like a corneal opacity or maybe an edema.
But the bulging lower eyelid when looking down makes me think about the lower eyelid structure.
When the lower eyelid bulges, especially when the patient looks down, it makes me consider a possible entrapment or something related to the lower lid.
I'm recalling that the lower eyelid is connected to the eye via the inferior eye muscles.
If there's a bulge, maybe it's due to an issue with the inferior tarsal muscle or the lower lid retractors.
Wait, could it be a case of ptosis?
Ptosis is when the eyelid droops, but the presentation here is a bulge when looking down, not just drooping at rest.
Maybe it's more specific than ptosis.
I'm thinking about the structure of the lower lid.
The lower lid is supported by the inferior orbital rim and the inferior tarsal muscle.
If there's a bulge, perhaps the muscle is not functioning properly, causing the lid to bulge out when the eye is moved downward.
Another thought: could it be a mechanical issue, like a foreign body causing the lid to bulge?
But the sudden pain and vision loss make me lean more towards a functional issue rather than something like a foreign body, which might present with more trauma or redness.
The hazy cornea could be due to edema, which might be related to the lid issue.
Maybe the lid is causing some pressure on the cornea, leading to edema.
Or perhaps the lid is so tight that it's causing the cornea to become edematous.
Wait, could it be a case of an entropion?
Entropion is when the eyelid turns inward, but the description here is a bulge, not an inward turn.
Maybe exotropion?
That's when the eyelid turns outward.
But exotropion usually refers to the eye turning outward, not the lid structure.
Hmm.
Alternatively, maybe it's a case of a lid abscess or cellulitis, but that usually presents with more redness and swelling, not necessarily a bulge when looking down.
Plus, the sudden vision loss could be due to an infection, but the lid issue seems more structural.
Wait, the bulging lower lid when looking down makes me think of the lower lid retractors.
If the inferior tarsal muscle is not functioning properly, the lid might not stay in its place, causing a bulge.
This could be due to a weakness or atrophy in that muscle, leading to a ptosis-like effect but specifically in the lower lid when the eye is moved.

So putting it all together, the sudden pain and vision loss with a hazy cornea and lower lid bulge when looking down point towards a structural issue with the lower eyelid, likely related to the inferior tarsal muscle or lower lid retractor.
This sounds like a case of ptosis, but more specifically, it's probably a type of lid ptosis or lower lid ptosis, which is a specific condition affecting the lower eyelid structure.

prompt: A 61-year-old female patient presents to your clinic due to sudden episodes of left-sided facial pain for the last two days. She states that the pain feels like a 'sharp stabbing ' and is a 9/10 in terms of intensity. The pain lasts about 5-10 seconds and then dissipates rapidly. The pain is often brought on by talking and cold wind. Her past medical history is significant for depression and type 2 DM.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out what's going on with this 61-year-old woman.
She's having these sudden episodes of left-sided facial pain.
The pain is described as sharp and stabbing, which is pretty intense—9/10 on the pain scale.
It only lasts for about 5-10 seconds before it goes away.
Interesting, so it's not a long-lasting pain, but it's pretty severe when it hits.
She mentions that the pain is triggered by talking and cold wind.
That's a bit specific.
I know that certain nerves can be affected by things like cold or pressure.
The left side is key here—so maybe it's related to the trigeminal nerve, which is on the same side as the pain.
The trigeminal nerve has three branches, and sometimes these can get inflamed, leading to pain.
That sounds like trigeminal neuralgia.
Her past medical history includes depression and type 2 DM.
Those aren't directly related to facial pain, but they might be red herrings or just part of her overall health.
I don't think they're causing the facial pain, but it's good to note for her overall care.
So putting it all together: sharp, left-sided facial pain, triggered by talking and cold wind, lasting seconds.
That fits with trigeminal neuralgia.
It's a common condition, though sometimes it's misdiagnosed as cluster headaches or other types of headaches.
But the triggers here—talking and cold—point more towards the trigeminal nerve.
...your internal reasoning for the diagnosis...
The patient describes sudden, sharp, left-sided facial pain triggered by talking and cold wind, which aligns with trigeminal neuralgia.
The pain's brief duration and specific triggers suggest this condition.

prompt: A 46-year-old woman with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection was seen by a clinician in Botswana (working in collaboration with members of a Massachusetts General Hospital [MGH] outreach program) because of postcoital bleeding. The patient had been generally well until 6 years before presentation, when weight loss and pelvic pain developed and she requested HIV testing at a government clinic. HIV-antibody testing was positive. Four years 3 months before presentation, the CD4+ T-cell count was 193 cells per cubic millimeter (Table 1), indicating that the patient was eligible for antiretroviral treatment (ART) in Botswana. The white-cell count was 3400 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range, 3900 to 8600), and the blood level of creatinine was 0.41 mg per deciliter (36 μmol per liter; reference range, 0.45 to 0.81 mg per deciliter [40 to 72 μmol per liter]). Two months later, treatment with a combination of tenofovir, emtricitabine, and efavirenz was begun. At a follow-up appointment 1 month later, a gynecologic examination was performed to evaluate vaginal discharge, urinary frequency, and dysuria. Abnormalities were reported, and administration of a 10-day course of amoxicillin was begun. Pathological examination of the specimen obtained during a screening Papanicolaou (Pap) test revealed a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion; however, the patient never received this result. Four months after the initiation of ART, the CD4+ T-cell count had improved (Table 1). Laboratory Data. One month later (5 months after the initiation of ART), the patient again reported dysuria; a course of nalidixic acid was administered. During the next 18 months, she continued to have recurrent pelvic pain, dysuria, and vaginal discharge. She sought care from traditional healers for these symptoms and postponed reporting the symptoms to her medical caregivers and undergoing a repeat Pap test, since she believed that the traditional therapies would help; the symptoms did not improve. Approximately 13 months before this presentation, the patient reported vaginal pruritus. Speculum examination revealed white patches on the cervix, and a repeat Pap test revealed a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. One month later, on review of the test results, colposcopic examination with biopsy was scheduled for the next available appointment, which was 14 months later. Approximately 10 months before this presentation, a small amount of vaginal bleeding reportedly occurred each time the patient had sexual intercourse; the patient was referred for gynecologic evaluation. One month before this presentation, the complete blood count, the creatinine level, and tests of liver function were normal; other results are shown inTable 1. She returned to the HIV clinic for evaluation. The patient reported no dyspareunia. She had undergone menarche at 15 years of age and first had sexual intercourse after the age of 17 years, and she was gravida 7, para 5. Medications included tenofovir, emtricitabine, and efavirenz; she had no known allergies. She lived in an urban area in Botswana with her five children and their father (who was also receiving ART for HIV infection). She did not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. She was employed periodically in a small shop. There was no family history of cancer. On examination, the abdomen was soft, without distention, rebound, or palpable masses. On pelvic examination, there were ulcers at the introitus; a malodorous, fungating lesion, 6 cm by 2 cm, on the right lateral vaginal wall, extending from the fornix to the introitus, with minimal bleeding on contact; and a nodular cervix. The remainder of the general examination was normal. Diagnostic procedures were performed.
true_dx: Condylomata acuminata and a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion of the cervix. Keratinizing squamous-cell carcinoma of the vagina. High-risk human papillomavirus infection.

Let's go through the information step by step.
The patient is a 46-year-old woman with HIV.
She presented with postcoital bleeding.
Before that, she had weight loss and pelvic pain, which led her to get tested for HIV six years ago.
Her CD4 count was 193, which is low enough to qualify for ART in Botswana.
She started treatment with tenofovir, emtricitabine, and efavirenz.
She had some gynecological issues too.
She was treated for a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) with amoxicillin, but she didn't follow up.
Later, she had recurrent pelvic pain, dysuria, and vaginal discharge.
She went to traditional healers instead of getting a repeat Pap test, which didn't help.
About a year later, she developed vaginal pruritus.
Her Pap test showed a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL).
She was referred for a colposcopy and biopsy, which was scheduled 14 months later.
She also had some vaginal bleeding during sex, but no dyspareunia.
On her last visit, her labs were normal, including CD4, creatinine, and liver function.
She had no dyspareunia.
Her pelvic exam showed ulcers at the introitus, a malodorous, fungating lesion on the right vaginal wall, and a nodular cervix.
Putting this together, the key symptoms are pelvic pain, dysuria, vaginal discharge, pruritus, and the findings on pelvic exam.
The lesion description sounds like it could be a fungal infection, especially with the malodorous and fungating nature.
Considering her HIV status and the treatment she's on, opportunistic infections are a concern.
Tenofovir is known to have side effects like increased risk of fungal infections, especially candidiasis.
The presence of a high-grade lesion and the clinical picture point towards a fungal infection, likely candidiasis.
The fact that she didn't respond to amoxicillin might indicate a different organism, but given the context, it's more likely a fungal infection.
So, the most likely diagnosis is candidiasis, specifically vaginal candidiasis or perhaps a more invasive form given the lesion size and description.

prompt: A 21-year-old man comes to the emergency room with swelling and severe pain in his left lower leg that started 2 hours ago. He has no history of serious illness or trauma. sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 21-year-old man who's presenting with left lower leg swelling and severe pain.

He's complaining of sudden swelling and pain in his left lower leg, which started two hours ago.
That makes me think it's an acute issue.
No prior serious illnesses or trauma, but his father has a history of pulmonary embolism, which is a significant clue.
Pulmonary embolism can lead to deep vein thrombosis (DVT) because when a blood clot breaks off and travels to the lungs, it can cause a DVT in the leg.
His physical exam shows a tender and swollen left lower leg, and dorsiflexion of the foot causes severe calf pain.
That's classic for DVT because when you flex the foot, it's a sign of calf muscle contraction, which can be painful if there's a blood clot.

Fibrin split products are positive, which suggests a clot is present.
The ultrasound of the left leg shows incompressibility of the popliteal vein with a hyperechoic mass and no blood flow.
Hyperechoic mass in ultrasound usually means a solid structure, like a tumor or a blood clot.
The incompressibility and absent blood flow point towards a DVT because the vein is blocked.

His symptoms, physical exam findings, and lab results all point to a deep vein thrombosis.

A 30-year-old man was seen in an outpatient clinic at this hospital because of fever and lymphadenopathy.
The patient had been well until approximately 2 weeks before presentation, when an enlarging, tender lump developed at the posterior base of the neck on the right side.
Two days before presentation, fever to a temperature of 39.4°C, a mild headache, myalgias, chills, and fatigue developed.
He took ibuprofen, but his condition did not improve, and he came to this hospital for evaluation.
The patient reported no history of sore throat, coryza, or earache.
He had had a low hemoglobin level in the past but was otherwise healthy.
He reportedly had had a negative tuberculin skin test in the past, and he had not received an influenza vaccine during the previous year.
He took no other medications and had no known allergies.
He was born in India and came to the United States 4 years previously to attend school; his most recent visit to India was 6 months before presentation.
He worked in an office and lived with a roommate.
He was not sexually active and had no known exposures to sick contacts, animals, or blood products.
He had stopped smoking 2 years before this presentation, drank alcohol occasionally, and did not use illicit drugs.
His parents had diabetes mellitus; there was no family history of autoimmune or connective-tissue diseases.
On examination, the temperature was 38.9°C, the blood pressure 129/80 mm
Hg, and the pulse 104 beats per minute.

A group of five tender lymph nodes, each approximately 1 cm in diameter, was present in the posteroinferior cervical chain on the right side; the lymph nodes in the posterior cervical chain on the left side and in both inguinal regions were nontender, and there were no abnormal lymph nodes in the supraclavicular or axillary regions.
A systolic ejection murmur (grade 1 out of 6) was heard at the cardiac base; the remainder of the examination was normal.
During evaluation, the temperature rose to 39.5°C and was associated with chills.

Blood levels of glucose, total protein, albumin, and globulin were normal, as were results of tests of liver and renal function; testing for heterophile antibodies and rapid tests for streptococcal pharyngitis and influenza virus were negative.
Additional test results are shown inTable 1.
A blood culture was sterile.
The administration of acetaminophen alternating with ibuprofen was recommended, as were fluids and rest.
The patient returned home but was advised to return to the outpatient clinic if his condition did not improve.

Two days later, the patient returned to the clinic.
He reported decreased appetite, chills, sweats related to fevers, mild headaches and body aches, and a new nonproductive cough.

On examination, the lymph nodes on the right side were slightly larger than on the previous examination and were slightly confluent; the lymph nodes on the left side and a submental lymph node were soft and mobile.
Bronchial breath sounds were heard over the right side of the chest anteriorly, and the remainder of the examination was unchanged.

The patient declined testing for the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).
A fine-needle aspiration biopsy of an enlarged cervical lymph node was performed, and the aspirate showed a mixed population of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and occasional plasma cells.
Some of the histiocytes contained cellular debris and angular, crescentic nuclei.
The polymorphous composition of the aspirate and the mature appearance of the lymphocytes were suggestive of a reactive process (Figure 1).
Gram's and acid-fast staining of the aspirate revealed no organisms.
Flow cytometry of the aspirate showed no immunophenotypic abnormalities.

Two days later, the patient reported persistent fevers and a dull headache and was admitted to the hospital.

prompt: A 50 year old chronic alcoholic male agricultural worker presented with high grade fever of one week duration with spells of chills and rigor. Examination of the respiratory system revealed bilateral crepitations with scattered rhonchi. Multiple subcutaneous nodules were found on the extensor surface of the left forearm, arm and left leg. Direct microscopy of the pus aspirated from the skin nodule revealed plenty of Gram negative bacilli with bipolar staining. Culture revealed distinct rough corrugated grey-white colonies on Blood agar. The organisms were motile and oxidase positive.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this case presentation.
Let's go through the information step by step.
The patient is a 50-year-old chronic alcoholic male who works in agriculture.
He's presenting with a high-grade fever for a week, along with chills and rigor.
That makes me think of an infection, maybe something like pneumonia or sepsis since those often cause high fevers and chills.
Looking at the respiratory exam, there are bilateral crepitations and scattered rhonchi.
Crepitations are crackles in the lungs, which can be seen in pneumonia, especially if it's bacterial.
Rhonchi are more common in bacterial infections than viral, so that supports a bacterial etiology.
Next, there are subcutaneous nodules on the left forearm, arm, and leg.
Subcutaneous nodules can be a sign of an infection spreading beyond the lungs, maybe abscesses or cellulitis.
The fact that they're on the extremities makes me think of a possible skin infection or something that's spread through the body.
The direct microscopy of the pus from the nodule shows Gram-negative bacilli with bipolar staining.
Gram-negative bacteria are a big clue.
They can cause a variety of infections, including bloodstream infections (like sepsis) or local infections like abscesses.
The bipolar staining is characteristic of certain bacteria, maybe like Staphylococcus aureus or another gram-negative organism.
The culture on blood agar shows rough, corrugated, grey-white colonies.
Blood agar is used for isolating bacteria, and the description of the colonies helps identify them.
Rough colonies might suggest certain species, like Staphylococcus or maybe some gram-negative bacteria like E. coli or Klebsiella.
The organisms are motile and oxidase positive.
Motile bacteria are typically gram-negative because gram-positive usually aren't motile.
Oxidase positive means they can use certain substrates for energy, which is a characteristic of some gram-negative bacteria like H influenzae or maybe even some enterobacteriaceae.

Putting it all together: the patient has a fever, respiratory symptoms pointing to pneumonia or sepsis, skin nodules suggesting a spreading infection, gram-negative bacteria with specific colony characteristics, and motility.
This makes me think of a gram-negative sepsis, possibly from an infection like E. coli or another such bacteria.
The presence of subcutaneous nodules could indicate that the infection has spread beyond the lungs, maybe through the bloodstream, leading to sepsis with skin involvement.
So, the most likely diagnosis here is gram-negative sepsis, likely caused by E. coli or another gram-negative organism given the microscopy and culture findings.
The patient's presentation of high fever, chills, respiratory symptoms, and skin nodules, combined with the microbiological findings of gram-negative bacilli, suggests gram-negative sepsis.
The presence of motile, oxidase-positive bacteria supports this diagnosis.

prompt: A 9 months old previously healthy infant was brought with complaints of fever of 12 hours' duration along with a running nose and an episode of generalized tonic clonic movements lasting for 34 minutes. Child was brought to the emergency within 1 hour. Child was observed in the emergency and was found to be alert active and playful after the fever came down.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 9-month-old infant.
Let's go through the information step by step.
The child is 9 months old and was previously healthy.
That's a good starting point because it means there are no prior health issues.
The main complaints are fever, running nose, and an episode of generalized tonic-clonic movements lasting 34 minutes.
The child was brought to the emergency within an hour, and after the fever went down, the child was alert, active, and playful.
First, the fever is a common symptom in many illnesses, so I need to consider what could cause a fever in an infant.
The running nose suggests a respiratory issue, maybe a cold or something similar.
The tonic-clonic movements, also known as a febrile seizure, are a big clue here.

I remember that febrile seizures typically occur in children between 6 months to 5 years of age, and they're usually associated with a fever, often from an infection like a viral upper respiratory infection, ear infection, or other bacterial or viral illnesses.
The fact that the child was brought in within an hour of the seizure is important.
I think that time frame is key because if it's a febrile seizure, it usually happens within the first 24 hours of the fever starting.

The child was observed and after the fever subsided, they became alert and playful, which aligns with the typical post-seizure behavior where the child might be tired or irritable right after the seizure but then becomes more active once the fever goes down.
I should also consider other possibilities.
Meningitis is a concern because it can cause fever, stiff neck, and altered mental status, but the child was alert after the fever went down, which makes me think it's less likely.
Encephalitis is another possibility, but again, the child's improvement after the fever suggests it's more of a febrile reaction rather than a more severe brain infection.
The running nose could be due to a viral infection, which is often the cause of febrile seizures.
So putting it all together, the most likely diagnosis is a febrile seizure caused by a viral upper respiratory infection or another similar infection.
I don't think it's a bacterial infection like meningitis because the child didn't have the typical signs like stiff neck or high fever that doesn't come down.
Also, the fact that the child was playful after the fever suggests it's a short-lived febrile reaction rather than something more chronic or severe.
So, the diagnosis is probably a febrile seizure due to a viral infection.
The child presented with fever, running nose, and a febrile seizure, typical of a viral infection causing a febrile reaction.

prompt: A 48-year-old man with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma was evaluated in the oncology clinic of this hospital because of abdominal pain. The patient had been generally well until 12 years before this presentation, when lymphadenopathy in the axillary and inguinal regions developed and a diagnosis of stage III follicular lymphoma was made. Rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone were administered and induced a clinical response; rituximab maintenance therapy was initiated. Seven years before this presentation, recurrent disease developed; rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, and prednisone were administered. The patient again had a clinical remission, and rituximab maintenance therapy was resumed. Two years before the current presentation, the patient transferred his oncologic care to this hospital. Swelling was noted in the right inguinal region, and18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron-emission tomography (PET) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed extensive FDG uptake throughout the body. Biopsy of a paraaortic lymph node revealed high-grade follicular lymphoma. Salvage chemotherapy with cisplatin, gemcitabine, rituximab, and dexamethasone was administered, and the patient had an early clinical remission. Four months later, and 20 months before the current presentation, the patient underwent autologous stem-cell transplantation after the administration of carmustine, cytarabine, etoposide, and melphalan. After transplantation, his clinical course was complicated by acute deep-vein thrombosis of the left leg; treatment with therapeutic enoxaparin sodium was initiated but was discontinued after 1 week owing to severe thrombocytopenia. Five months later, clinical signs of lymphoma relapse were observed, and biopsy of an enlarged axillary lymph node revealed transformation to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The patient was subsequently treated with several therapies, including blinatumomab, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells, and pembrolizumab, none of which induced a sustained clinical response. Because of the lack of clinical response, allogeneic stem-cell transplantation was considered. Two and a half weeks before this presentation, the patient was admitted to this hospital for severe pain in the epigastrium and bilateral inguinal regions. Laboratory studies revealed a lactate dehydrogenase level of 1560 U per liter (reference range, 110 to 210), an alanine aminotransferase level of 127 U per liter (reference range, 10 to 55), an aspartate aminotransferase level of 143 U per liter (reference range, 10 to 40), an alkaline phosphatase level of 1506 U per liter (reference range, 30 to 100), and a total bilirubin level of 2.5 mg per deciliter (reference range, 0.0 to 1.0). Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, performed after the administration of intravenous contrast material, revealed several clustered small pulmonary nodules, progressive hepatosplenomegaly with normal-appearing bile ducts, multifocal enlarging lymph nodes, and new small-volume ascites. Oral methadone and morphine sulfate and a 5-day course of intravenous methylprednisolone were administered, resulting in alleviation of pain and improvement in liver function. The patient was discharged home on the fifth hospital day. Two weeks after discharge, the patient was evaluated in the oncology clinic of this hospital for recurrent severe, sharp pain in the bilateral inguinal regions, as well as diffuse abdominal pain in the upper quadrants that was no longer responsive to oral analgesic agents. He had no known allergies to medications. The patient was born and raised in central Mexico and often returned to visit family. He had moved to the United States 2 years before this presentation. He lived with his wife and two adolescent daughters in an urban neighborhood in New England. He worked in the information technology industry. He had previously smoked one cigarette daily and had quit 4 years earlier; he drank one beer every other week and did not use illicit drugs. His mother had had breast cancer, and his father had had coronary artery disease, hypertension, and alcohol use disorder. His children were healthy. The weight was 61.5 kg, and the body-mass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) 20.0. He had cachexia and was in moderate distress from pain. The mucous membranes were dry, and thrush was present in the oropharynx. The abdomen was soft, with normal bowel sounds; the right and left upper quadrants were moderately tender on palpation. Painful lymphadenopathy involving the cervical, supraclavicular, and inguinal chains was present. The patient was oriented to person, place, and time, and no confusion was noted. There was no rash. sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the most likely diagnosis for this patient.
Let's start by going through the case presentation step by step.
The patient is a 48-year-old man with a history of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
He initially had follicular lymphoma, which progressed to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
He's been through several treatments, including rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone, as well as maintenance therapy.
He had a relapse and underwent autologous stem-cell transplantation, but then developed acute deep-vein thrombosis, which complicated his recovery.
After that, he relapsed again and was treated with blinatumomab, CAR T cells, and pembrolizumab without a sustained response.
Now, he's back in the hospital with severe abdominal pain, night sweats, decreased energy, poor appetite, nausea, and constipation.
Looking at his lab results, his LDH is elevated at 1560 U/L, which is way above the normal range.
His ALT and AST are also high, indicating liver dysfunction.
His alkaline phosphatase is significantly elevated, which can suggest either liver disease or bone issues.
His total bilirubin is 2.5 mg/dL, which is elevated, but the direct bilirubin is 3.8 mg/dL, which is even higher.
This points towards either prehepatic or hepatocellular issues.
His albumin is low at 2.5 g/dl, which can be due to inflammation or liver disease.
The imaging studies show multiple small pulmonary nodules, hepatosplenomegaly, and new small-volume ascites.
The CT abdomen shows multiple hypodense lesions in the liver and bilateral pleural effusions.
The MRI of the liver confirms these lesions with hyperintensity on T2-weighted imaging and no enhancement, which is typical for microabscesses or lymphomatous deposits.
He also developed shaking chills and a fever after a platelet transfusion, which could indicate an infection.
His mental status changed, but it returned to baseline the next morning.
On the second hospital day, he still had abdominal pain and low-grade fever, and his labs showed an elevated ammonia level, which can be seen in liver disease or encephalopathy.
His lipase and amylase are also elevated, suggesting possible cholecystitis or pancreatitis, but the imaging didn't show bile duct dilation, so it's more likely related to the liver.
Putting this all together, the patient has a history of lymphoma, which can involve the liver and spleen.
The imaging findings of multiple liver lesions with hyperintensity on T2 and no enhancement are consistent with microabscesses or lymphomatous deposits.
The elevated LDH, AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase support liver dysfunction.
The presence of hepatosplenomegaly and ascites also points towards liver involvement.
Considering his history of lymphoma, the most likely diagnosis here is lymphoma relapse involving the liver and spleen.
The transformation to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after initial follicular lymphoma is also a factor, as this type can have aggressive behavior and can involve multiple organs, including the liver.

The other possibilities mentioned in the imaging, like hepatosplenic microabscesses, are less likely because the patient's history and the clinical presentation are more consistent with lymphoma progression.
Additionally, the lack of dilated bile ducts makes cholangitis less likely, and the patient's history of cancer makes lymphoma the primary suspect.
Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is relapsed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with liver and spleen involvement.

prompt: A previously healthy 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of upper back pain, dyspnea, and a sensation of pressure in his chest. He has had no shortness of breath, palpitations, fevers, or chills. He emigrated from Ecuador when he was 5 years old. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. He takes no medications. He is 194 cm (6 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 70.3 kg (155 lb); BMI is 19 kg/m2. His temperature is 37.2В°C (99.0В°F), pulse is 73/min, respirations are 15/min, and blood pressure is 152/86 mm Hg in the right arm and 130/72 mg Hg in the left arm. Pulmonary examination shows faint inspiratory wheezing bilaterally. A CT scan of the chest with contrast is shown. What is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 32-year-old man with a week-long history of upper back pain, dyspnea, and chest pressure.
He's been feeling a bit unwell, but he doesn't have the usual signs like fevers or chills.
He's a non-smoker, doesn't drink, and isn't on any medications.
His vitals are slightly elevated in blood pressure, but not super high.
He's tall and a bit underweight, but his BMI is 19, which is within the normal range.
He's had a CT scan of the chest with contrast, and the results are important here.
The pulmonary exam shows faint wheezing on both sides, which suggests some obstruction or narrowing in the airways.
Since he's a migrant from Ecuador, maybe there's something environmental or something he's exposed to there that's causing this.
I'm thinking about possible causes.
The upper back pain and chest pressure could point towards something like a pulmonary issue, maybe a chronic condition.
The wheezing makes me think of asthma or maybe something like COPD, but those are more chronic.
However, he's only been symptomatic for a week, so maybe it's an acute issue.
Another thought is that it could be related to a parasitic infection.
Places like Ecuador have a high incidence of parasites like roundworms, which can cause pulmonary issues.
The upper back pain might be from the worms migrating through the tissues.
The chest pressure and dyspnea could be due to a pulmonary infestation.
The CT scan would show opacities or changes in the lungs that are consistent with parasitic infection.
Maybe the contrast would highlight any abnormal areas where the parasites are affecting the lung tissue.
So putting it all together, the most likely diagnosis is parasitic pneumonia, probably caused by a parasitic worm like Ascaris lumbricoides, which is common in regions where he's been.
The migration of the worms could explain the back pain and the pulmonary symptoms.

The patient's symptoms, including upper back pain, dyspnea, and chest pressure, along with the presence of wheezing and his history of migration from a region with high parasitic prevalence, point towards a parasitic infection.
The CT scan likely shows findings consistent with parasitic pneumonia, such as Ascaris lumbricoides infection.

prompt: A 19 years old young girl with previous history of repeated pain over medial canthus and chronic use of nasal decongestants, presented with abrupt onset of fever with chills and rigor, diplopia on lateral gaze, moderate proptosis and chemosis. On examination optic disc is congested.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 19-year-old girl.
Let me go through the information step by step.
First, the patient is a young woman with a history of repeated pain over the medial canthus.
Medial canthus is the area near the inner corner of the eye, so that makes me think of possible issues related to the eye, maybe something like an infection or inflammation.
She's been using nasal decongestants chronically.
I know that decongestants can cause side effects, especially if used for a long time.
They can lead to rebound congestion, but I'm not sure how that ties into her current symptoms.
She presents with an abrupt onset of fever, chills, and rigor.
Those are classic signs of a systemic infection, like a bacterial or viral infection.
Fever and chills usually point towards something like a sinus infection, maybe sinusitis, which can cause these systemic symptoms.
Then there's diplopia on lateral gaze.
Diplopia is double vision, often due to issues with the eye muscles or the nerves controlling them.
Lateral gaze specifically refers to moving the eyes side to side, so this could indicate a problem with the lateral rectus muscles or the third cranial nerve, which controls that movement.
She also has moderate proptosis.
Proptosis is the forward protrusion of the eye, which can be caused by inflammation or edema of the orbital tissues.
This makes me think of orbital cellulitis, an infection in the eye socket that can cause the eye to bulge out.
Chemosis is another clue.
Chemosis refers to inflammation or swelling of the conjunctiva, the thin layer covering the white part of the eye.
This is often seen in infections like bacterial or viral conjunctivitis.
The optic disc is congested.

A congested optic disc can be seen in conditions like papilledema, which is swelling of the optic nerve head, commonly associated with increased intracranial pressure or conditions like papilledema due to infections or inflammations.
Putting this all together: she has a history of eye issues, using decongestants, and now presenting with systemic symptoms of fever, diplopia, proptosis, chemosis, and a congested optic disc.
The diplopia and proptosis point towards an orbital infection, possibly orbital cellulitis.
The fever and other systemic symptoms suggest that this infection might be spreading beyond just the orbit, maybe into the sinuses or causing a systemic response.
Orbital cellulitis is often caused by bacteria, and if it's severe, it can lead to complications like abscess formation.
The use of nasal decongestants might have contributed by causing sinusitis, which can lead to orbital infections if not treated properly.
So, considering all these points, the most likely diagnosis is orbital cellulitis.

It explains the eye symptoms, the systemic signs, and the possible connection to her previous use of decongestants.

No organisms were seen on periodic acid–Schiff staining, Gram’s staining, or staining for acid-fast bacilli. Doxycycline was prescribed. The patient traveled to Jordan and stayed for 4 weeks; during that time, the lesion on the left side of the chin receded, the lesion on the right forearm doubled in size, and the lesion on the left forearm recurred. Clusters of painful vulvovaginal ulcers developed; these waxed and waned. In the infectious disease clinic, the patient reported a 5-month history of waxing and waning skin lesions, a 2-month history of episodic vulvovaginal ulcers, and occasional nausea. She had a history of attention-deficit disorder. She took a combination birth control pill daily. Her father had diabetes mellitus, and her mother had hypertension and polymyalgia rheumatica. The patient was of European descent. She was a graduate student and traveled abroad frequently for internships. While she was in Morocco 11 months earlier, she rode on a camel; while she was in Thailand, she petted an elephant and swam in freshwater waterfall pools. She had not visited farms or milked animals and had no known sick contacts. She had been sexually active for several years with one partner, who used condoms. On examination, the temperature was 36.5°C, the blood pressure 90/52 mm Hg, the pulse 66 beats per minute, the respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and the oxygen saturation 99% while the patient was breathing ambient air. sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 10-year-old boy with a 3-month history of headaches.

prompt: A 68-year-old man was seen in the cancer center at this hospital because of metastatic melanoma. Eleven years earlier, a superficial spreading melanoma had been excised from the right lower leg. The patient had been well until approximately 5 weeks before presentation to this hospital, when pain and swelling developed in the right leg and groin. Four weeks before presentation, he was seen in the emergency department at another hospital. Examination revealed a mass in the right groin, with surrounding erythema. A course of cephalexin was administered, with resolution of pain and erythema but persistence of the mass. Computed tomography (CT) of the pelvis reportedly revealed an irregular mass (3.1 cm in diameter) in the right groin. One week later, combination positron-emission tomography (PET) and CT (PET-CT) reportedly revealed hypermetabolic lymph nodes involving the right external iliac, femoral, and inguinal regions, and the medial right thigh. Eight days before presentation to this hospital, an ultrasound-guided biopsy of a lymph node in the right groin was performed at the other hospital. Pathological examination showed metastatic melanoma. The patient was referred to the cancer center at this hospital. The patient reported feeling well, with no pain, fatigue, nausea, weight loss, headaches, cough, or dyspnea. He had a history of hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux disease, diverticulitis, cardiomyopathy, coronary artery disease (he had undergone placement of a stent 1 year earlier), and hearing loss. He had a history of extensive sun exposure. Medications included aspirin, metoprolol, digoxin, hydrochlorothiazide, valsartan, clopidogrel, and a multivitamin, as well as acetaminophen and nitroglycerin spray, as needed. He had no known allergies. He lived with his wife and was retired, having previously worked as a landscaper and mechanic. He remained physically active, performing farm work. He had smoked three packs of cigarettes daily for 20 years (stopping 20 years earlier), drank alcohol infrequently, and did not use illicit drugs. His sister had had uterine cancer, and his maternal grandmother had had breast cancer; there was no family history of melanoma. On examination, the blood pressure was 151/87 mm Hg; other vital signs and the oxygen saturation level while the patient was breathing ambient air were normal. Hearing was decreased, and a hearing aide was noted in the right ear. Masses were present in the right groin and right medial thigh, measuring 6 cm and 5 cm in maximal dimension, respectively. There was mild erythema and swelling of the right thigh and a well-healed scar on the right calf. There was no palpable cervical, supraclavicular, submental, occipital, or axillary adenopathy. The blood glucose level was 56 mg per deciliter (3.1 mmol per liter; reference range, 70 to 110 mg per deciliter [3.9 to 6.1 mmol per liter]). A complete blood count, the prothrombin time, and the results of tests of renal and liver function were normal, as were blood levels of electrolytes, total protein, albumin, and globulin. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed enlarged retroperitoneal, pelvic sidewall, and inguinal lymph nodes on the right side, with the largest lymph node (4 cm in diameter) in the right groin (Figure 1A). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head revealed nonspecific changes and no mass lesion. The procedure was terminated before the administration of gadolinium because of claustrophobia. Imaging Studies.A CT image of the abdomen and pelvis on initial evaluation (Panel A) shows a large mass in the right groin (arrow). A repeat CT image obtained 39 weeks after the start of treatment with vemurafenib (Panel B) shows new metastatic lesions in the spine (arrow) and a compression fracture (arrowhead). An image from MRI of the brain shows new enhancing masses consistent with metastasis (Panel C, arrow). During stereotactic radiosurgery for a left frontal metastasis (Panel D), the patient received 1800 cGy to the volume delineated by the green isodose line. An image from a repeat MRI scan obtained 11 months later (Panel E) shows nearly complete resolution of brain lesions (arrow). A CT image from a combination positron-emission tomographic and CT scan of the whole body obtained 1 month later (Panel F) reveals resolution of inguinal lymphadenopathy (arrow). One week later, a diagnostic test was performed and management decisions were made.

prompt: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she has not attained menarche. There is no personal or family history of serious illness. She is 168 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 63 kg (139 lb); BMI is 22.3 kg/m2. Examination shows normal breast development. Scant axillary hair is present. Abdominal examination shows a firm, nontender left inguinal mass. Pelvic examination shows a blind vaginal pouch. Ultrasonography does not show a uterus or ovaries. What is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 17-year-old girl who hasn't had her period yet.
Let me go through the information step by step.
First, she's 17 and hasn't attained menarche, which means she's anadrogenous, not having started menstruating yet.
That's a bit concerning because usually, by 16-18 years old, most girls have started their periods.
So, something is delaying that.
Her height is 168 cm, which is about 5 feet 5 inches, and she weighs 63 kg.
Her BMI is 22.3, which is just slightly above the normal weight range (usually 18.5-25 is normal).
So she's within a healthy weight range, not underweight or overweight.
On examination, she has normal breast development.
That's interesting because sometimes in cases of disorders like Turner syndrome, breast development can be delayed or absent.
But here, her breasts are normal, so that might point away from Turner syndrome.
She has scant axillary hair.
Usually, in cases of hypothyroidism or Turner syndrome, there can be decreased axillary hair.
But again, she has some, so maybe not the most indicative sign.
The abdominal examination shows a firm, nontender left inguinal mass.
That's a key finding.
A firm mass in the inguinal area could be a testicular or ovarian mass.
Since the pelvic exam shows a blind vaginal pouch, that suggests that the uterus might be absent or not functional.
Wait, the ultrasound didn't show a uterus or ovaries.
So, no uterus and no ovaries?
That's a big clue.
Wait, if the ultrasound didn't show a uterus or ovaries, that suggests that she might have a congenital absence of these structures.
But she's 17, so maybe she has a condition where she didn't develop these organs.
The blind vaginal pouch could be due to the absence of the uterus, leading to the vaginal canal being closed off, hence the pouch.
The lack of a uterus and ovaries points towards a condition called Mayer-Vicker's syndrome.
I remember that Mayer-Vicker's is a type of congenital disorder where the female doesn't have a uterus, ovaries, or fallopian tubes.
It's a rare condition, and these girls typically present with primary amenorrhea, which is what this patient has.
Also, the inguinal mass could be due to an inguinal hernia, but the fact that the mass is firm and nontender makes me think it's more structural, like a congenital absence leading to a blind pouch.
In Mayer-Vicker's, sometimes there's an inguinal hernia because the abdominal muscles aren't pulling in, which can cause an inguinal mass.
Putting it all together: no uterus, no ovaries, blind vaginal pouch, and primary amenorrhea.
Mayer-Vicker's syndrome fits all these findings.
It's a rare condition, but the absence of reproductive organs explains the lack of menarche and the other physical signs.
The patient's presentation of primary amenorrhea, absence of reproductive organs on ultrasound, and a blind vaginal pouch along with a firm inguinal mass is indicative of Mayer-Vicker's syndrome.

prompt: A 23-year-old woman is noticed to have irregular pupils on routine examination. She has 1 large pupil, which has minimal response to light stimulation, but it does respond to accommodation. The eye movements are normal and she experiences no double vision.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 23-year-old woman with irregular pupils.
Let me start by breaking down the information given.
First, she has one large pupil that doesn't respond to light stimulation.
Wait, but it does respond to accommodation.
Hmm, I remember that the pupil size is controlled by the autonomic nervous system, specifically the parasympathetic system.
When the pupil is large, it's usually because the parasympathetic fibers are active, which happens in bright light.
But in this case, the pupil doesn't respond to light, which is odd because normally, in bright light, the pupil should constrict.
Wait, but it does respond to accommodation.
Accommodation refers to the eye's ability to adjust the lens shape to focus on objects at different distances.
So, the pupil is responsive to changes in object distance, but not to light.
That makes me think of a condition where the pupil is stuck in a certain state.
I recall that in Horner's syndrome, the pupil is constricted, but that's the opposite of what's happening here.
Maybe it's the opposite of Horner's?
Or perhaps something else.
Oh, Adie's syndrome comes to mind.
Adie's syndrome is characterized by a large, non-reactive pupil that doesn't respond to light but does respond to accommodation.
That fits the description here.
Adie's syndrome is usually associated with an absence of parasympathetic innervation to the eye.
It's often idiopathic but can be associated with other conditions like brain lesions or trauma.
The fact that her eye movements are normal and she doesn't have double vision suggests that the issue is with the pupil control, not the eye movements themselves.
So, putting it all together, the large, non-reactive pupil that responds to accommodation points towards Adie's syndrome.
I don't think it's Horner's because that's a different type of pupil response.
Also, no double vision indicates that the oculomotor muscles are functioning normally, so it's not a neurological issue affecting eye movement control.
The patient exhibits a large, non-reactive pupil that responds to accommodation, indicating Adie's syndrome.
This condition is characterized by loss of parasympathetic innervation to the eye, leading to a fixed, dilated pupil that doesn't react to light but accommodates for distance changes.

prompt: A 53-year-old white woman with end-stage renal disease received a kidney transplant and was maintained on an immunosuppressive regimen. Three months later she had a fever (38.3degC) and was found to have acute renal failure. Renal transplant biopsy was performed.
