A stool test was positive for occult blood, and a diagnostic colonoscopy was scheduled. Laboratory Data. Three days before admission, the patient felt feverish but did not check his temperature at home. Fevers continued, despite the use of acetaminophen. One day before admission, he had one episode of nonbloody, nonbilious vomiting. On the day of admission, the patient had an unwitnessed fall while he was standing in the bathroom; he reported that he had felt generally weak and had tried to sit down but fell backward and struck his head, without loss of consciousness. He was found on the floor by a family member and was unable to stand up. He was brought to the emergency department of this hospital. On evaluation in the emergency department, the patient reported generalized myalgias but no headache, photophobia, or neck stiffness. He had a history of hypertension, non–insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, and vitamin D deficiency. Medications included lisinopril and aspirin; the diabetes was controlled by diet. He had no family history of cancer or autoimmune disease. He had not smoked tobacco in 30 years but had previously smoked 1 pack of cigarettes per day for 20 years. He drank alcohol occasionally and did not use illicit drugs. He was retired, resided in New England, and had not traveled outside the region in several years. He did not have pets or known exposures to bats. He had recently cleaned out the basement of his home, where he had occasionally seen mice. On examination, the temperature was 38.9°C, the blood pressure 140/64 mm Hg, the pulse 83 beats per minute, the respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and the oxygen saturation 94% while the patient was breathing ambient air. He was diaphoretic but did not appear ill. He was alert and oriented, and he answered questions appropriately. Examination of cranial nerves II through XII was normal. Strength and sensation to light touch were intact in the arms and legs. Deep-tendon reflexes in the arms and legs were normal; the plantar reflex was flexor bilaterally. Computed tomography of the head, chest, abdomen, and pelvis was performed without the administration of intravenous contrast material. Mild circumferential thickening of the middle and distal esophagus was noted. No focal hepatic lesions, thickening or distention of the gastrointestinal tract, or suspicious lytic or blastic lesions of the bones were noted. The patient was admitted to the hospital. During the next 12 hours, altered mental status developed, with progressive confusion, difficulties with word finding, and inability to consistently follow commands. Several attempts at lumbar puncture for analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were unsuccessful, and empirical treatment with intravenous vancomycin, ceftriaxone, ampicillin, and acyclovir was initiated. Additional studies were obtained. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head was performed with and without the administration of intravenous contrast material. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images showed scattered foci of signal abnormalities in the supratentorial white matter, with no evidence of intracranial mass, hemorrhage, or acute infarction. Electroencephalography revealed intermittent irregular delta slowing that was most prominent in the left frontocentral area and intermittent diffuse theta slowing in the background, with no epileptiform abnormalities. On the second hospital day, a lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 19.5 cm of water; other results are shown inTable 1. Doxycycline was administered orally. Fevers continued, despite the administration of acetaminophen. The blood cultures had no growth. Progressive tachypnea developed, and the patient was unable to lie in a recumbent position to undergo repeat MRI of the head. Elective intubation was performed, and mechanical ventilation was initiated. On the fourth hospital day, repeat MRI of the head was performed. FLAIR images showed new mild, diffuse hyperintensity in the sulci, and FLAIR and T2-weighted images showed mild hyperintensity in the medial thalami and medial temporal lobes (Figure 1). MRI of the Head.MRI of the head was performed on the fourth hospital day. There is mild hyperintensity in the medial temporal lobes (Panel A, arrows) and the thalami (Panels B and C, arrowheads), as well as mildly increased signal in the sulci, most notably in the sylvian fissures (Panel B, arrows). There are scattered hyperintense foci in the white matter, most prominently in the left corona radiata (Panel D, arrow). Physical examination, which was performed while the patient was not receiving sedation, revealed decreased tone and no spontaneous movements of the arms or legs, findings consistent with flaccid paralysis. There was also no withdrawal in response to nail-bed pressure, and deep-tendon reflexes were absent in the arms, knees, and ankles bilaterally. The patient opened his eyes but did not regard or track the examiner and did not respond to requests. The diameter of the pupils was 3 mm bilaterally and decreased to 2 mm in response to bright light. The corneal reflexes and cough reflex were intact, but there was no grimace in response to pressure in the supraorbital notch. On the 10th hospital day, nerve-conduction studies were performed. The sensory responses of the left median and ulnar nerves were prolonged and had moderately-to-severely reduced amplitude, and the motor responses of the bilateral median nerves had severely reduced amplitude, normal conduction velocities, and normal durations. Stimulation of the muscles by means of needle electromyography revealed abundant fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves in the left deltoid, extensor digitorum communis, first dorsal interosseous, and tibialis anterior muscles, as well as increased insertional activity in the left vastus lateralis and medial gastrocnemius muscles and no voluntary motor units in the left arm or leg. A diagnostic test was performed.

prompt: A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because of coughing and fatigue during the past 2 years. In the morning, the cough is productive of white phlegm. She becomes short of breath walking up a flight of stairs. She has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. She has recently retired from working as a nurse at a homeless shelter. She has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. Current medications include ramipril and fenofibrate. Her temperature is 36.5В°C (97.7В°F), respirations are 24/min, pulse is 85/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Scattered wheezing and rhonchi are heard throughout both lung fields. There are no murmurs, rubs, or gallops but heart sounds are distant. What is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?

Let me go through the information step by step.
She's been coughing and feeling fatigued for two years.
The cough is worse in the morning and brings up white phlegm.
That makes me think of chronic bronchitis or maybe something like COPD because chronic cough with phlegm is a common symptom.
She also has trouble breathing when walking up stairs, which points towards a respiratory issue that's affecting her daily activities.
She has hypertension and hyperlipidemia, which are risk factors for cardiovascular diseases, but her primary complaint is respiratory.
She used to work as a nurse at a homeless shelter, which might expose her to various infections, but I'm not sure if that's directly relevant here.
She smokes a pack a day for 40 years.
That's a significant smoking history, which is a major risk factor for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), emphysema, or lung cancer.
Her current medications include ramipril, which is an ACE inhibitor used for hypertension and maybe heart failure, and fenofibrate, which is for hyperlipidemia.
So, she has some cardiovascular risk factors as well.
Her vital signs are within normal range except for her blood pressure, which is 140/90.
That's a bit on the higher side but not critically high.
Her respiratory rate is 24, which is a bit elevated, but not super high.
She has scattered wheezing and rhonchi in both lung fields, which suggests lower respiratory tract obstruction or inflammation, like in asthma or COPD.

She doesn't have murmurs, rubs, or gallops, so heart issues are less likely the primary problem unless it's something silent, but her distant heart sounds make me think the heart isn't the main issue here.
Putting it all together: smoking history, chronic cough with phlegm, wheezing, and respiratory distress on exertion.
This points towards a chronic respiratory condition.
Given her age and smoking history, COPD is the most likely diagnosis.
It's a common condition in smokers and fits all her symptoms: chronic cough, phlegm, wheezing, and reduced exercise tolerance.
The patient's history of chronic cough with white phlegm, wheezing, and smoking history, along with her age, suggests a diagnosis of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD).

prompt: A 59-year-old man was evaluated in the rheumatology clinic of this hospital because of headache and progressive neurologic dysfunction. Ten months before this evaluation, daily fever with a temperature of up to 38.9°C, chills, myalgias, drenching night sweats, and pressure and pain in both cheeks and ears developed. The patient was evaluated by his primary care physician. He reported rhinorrhea and fatigue but no headache, pharyngitis, or dyspnea, and he had no sick contacts. On examination, the temperature was 37.8°C, the heart rate 100 beats per minute, the blood pressure 112/64 mm Hg, and the oxygen saturation 98% while he was breathing ambient air. He was ill-appearing, and the maxillary sinuses were tender on palpation; the remainder of the examination was normal. Blood levels of electrolytes, calcium, total protein, albumin, and globulin were normal, as were the results of kidney-function tests. The platelet count was 463,000 per microliter (reference range, 140,000 to 400,000); the remainder of the complete blood count and the differential count were normal. Amoxicillin–clavulanate was prescribed. During the next 2 weeks, fever, night sweats, and sinus and facial pain continued. Diffuse headache developed, along with jaw soreness, scalp tenderness, and hip and shoulder stiffness. The patient was evaluated again by his primary care physician. He reported weight loss of 2 kg, episodic double vision, and hip pain that caused difficulty in standing and climbing stairs. The physical examination was unchanged. Urinalysis was normal. A test for heterophile antibody and an interferon-γ release assay forMycobacterium tuberculosiswere negative, as were screening tests for human immunodeficiency virus and Lyme disease. Chest radiography and computed tomography of the sinuses were normal. The patient was referred to a rheumatologist at another hospital. On evaluation, the patient reported persistent fever and frontal, temporal, and maxillary headache. There were palpable temporal artery pulses without tenderness; the remainder of the examination was normal, including the absence of bruits on auscultation of large vessels. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 108 mm per hour (reference range, 0 to 20), the blood level of C-reactive protein greater than 100 mg per liter (reference value, <8.0), the blood level of rheumatoid factor 24 IU per milliliter (reference value, <14), and the blood level of aldolase 8.4 IU per milliliter (reference value, <8.1). Biopsy of the right temporal artery was performed. Histologic examination of the biopsy specimen reportedly showed no granulomas, but evidence of chronic inflammation of the temporal artery and fibrinoid necrosis of an adjacent small vessel were noted. A diagnosis of giant-cell arteritis was made, and treatment with prednisone was started. Within a few days after initiation of treatment, headache, fever, jaw pain, and joint stiffness abated. The next month, an attempt to lower the prednisone dose resulted in recurrent severe headache with scalp tenderness, jaw pain, and hip stiffness. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 55 mm per hour and the C-reactive protein level 84 mg per liter. Treatment with weekly subcutaneous administration of tocilizumab was initiated. During the next 6 weeks, another attempt was made to taper the prednisone dose. After 1 week of treatment at a lower prednisone dose, and 5 months after the development of initial symptoms (5 months before the current evaluation), the patient reported headache that he described as “the worst headache of my life,” with associated jaw pain and diplopia. The pain was worst at the right frontal and maxillary areas, but the entire right side of the face, including the scalp and neck, was affected. The patient returned to the other hospital for evaluation. He was found to have palsies of the third and sixth cranial nerves on the right side. The patient was admitted to the neurology service at the other hospital. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) testing revealed a slightly elevated myeloperoxidase antibody level, at 1.9 U (reference value, <1.0), but antibodies to proteinase 3 were not detected. Blood levels of IgG subclasses were normal. Imaging studies were obtained. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head (Figure 1A and 1B), performed after the administration of intravenous contrast material, revealed abnormal expansion and enhancement of the right cavernous sinus that extended into the right superior orbital fissure and right pterygopalatine fossa, as well as abnormal pachymeningeal thickening and enhancement of the adjacent right middle cranial fossa. MRI of the cervical spine (Figure 1C and 1D) showed masslike pachymeningeal thickening and enhancement in the upper cervical spinal canal at C2–C4 with an anterior predominance as well as more circumferentially at the cervicothoracic junction (C6–T3) with a posterior predominance, with resultant canal narrowing and mild cord compression at C7–T2. There was no spinal cord edema. MRI of the Head and Spine Obtained 5 Months before the Current Evaluation.Axial and coronal contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images of the head (Panels A and B, respectively) show abnormal enhancement of the right cavernous sinus that extends into the right superior orbital fissure and adjacent right middle cranial fossa (arrows). Sagittal and axial contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images of the cervical spine with fat suppression (Panels C and D, respectively) show abnormal pachymeningeal enhancement and thickening anteriorly in the upper cervical spinal canal at C2–C4 as well as more circumferentially with a posterior predominance at the cervicothoracic junction, with resultant variable canal stenosis and mild cord compression (arrows). A lumbar puncture was performed; an opening pressure was not recorded. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) glucose level was 65 mg per deciliter (3.6 mmol per liter; reference range, 50 to 80 mg per deciliter [2.8 to 4.4 mmol per liter]), and the protein level was 126 mg per deciliter (reference range, 15 to 45), with 2 red cells per microliter and 8 white cells per microliter (of which 79% were lymphocytes). Gram’s staining and cultures of the CSF were negative. Tests for CSF myelin basic protein, angiotensin-converting enzyme, cryptococcal antigen, cysticercosis IgG, mycobacterial DNA, Epstein–Barr virus DNA, and borrelia DNA were negative, as was a Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test. Cytologic analysis of the CSF showed a mixed population of mononuclear cells with rare plasma cells. The CSF immunoglobulin level was 19 mg per deciliter (reference range, 0 to 6), with 5 oligoclonal bands. On the eighth hospital day, a meningeal biopsy was performed. Treatment with high-dose prednisone was started, and the patient was discharged home. During the next 2 weeks, the patient continued taking the prednisone, but the facial and head pain worsened. He was readmitted to the other hospital to receive 3 days of treatment with parenteral pulse-dose methylprednisolone. Pathological examination of the meningeal biopsy specimen revealed a densely fibrotic, chronically inflamed dura mater with large numbers of CD68+ macrophages and CD3+ T lymphocytes and with focal collections of CD20+ B lymphocytes. There was a large number of polyclonal plasma cells with more than 100 IgG4+ plasma cells per high-power field. Storiform fibrosis was present, and elastin staining revealed obliterative venulitis. Some of the inflammatory foci were angiocentric, but no vasculitis was present. There were rare foci of fibrinoid necrosis and some neutrophils, with rare giant cells but no granulomas. A diagnosis of IgG4-related disease was made, and rituximab was administered. Two days after the first rituximab dose, a pulmonary embolism was diagnosed, and treatment with apixaban was initiated. Two weeks later, repeat imaging was obtained to evaluate the treatment response. Repeat MRI of the head (Figure 2A and 2B), performed after the administration of intravenous contrast material, revealed increased abnormal enhancement in the right cavernous sinus and right middle cranial fossa and new abnormal enhancement in the left cavernous sinus and adjacent left middle cranial fossa. MRI of the cervical spine (Figure 2C and 2D) also showed progression in the extent and thickness of the ventral and dorsal pachymeningeal thickening and enhancement. There was also progression of the canal stenosis, which had become severe, and cord compression at the C7 level. There was no cord signal abnormality. MRI of the Head and Spine Obtained 4 Months before the Current Evaluation.Repeat head and spinal MRI studies were obtained 2 weeks after treatment with rituximab was initiated. Axial and coronal contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images of the head (Panels A and B, respectively) show increased abnormal enhancement on the right side (arrows) and new abnormal enhancement in the left cavernous sinus and left middle cranial fossa (arrowheads). Sagittal and axial contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images of the cervical spine with fat suppression (Panels C and D, respectively) show progression of the abnormal pachymeningeal enhancement with worsening canal stenosis and progressive cord compression but no cord signal abnormality (arrows). The patient received a second infusion of rituximab, as well as treatment with oral dexamethasone. Three weeks later, and 7 months after the development of initial symptoms (3 months before the current evaluation), the patient was admitted to the other hospital because of worsening headache, nausea, and vomiting. Examination was notable for new sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear and deviation of the tongue to the left. A ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed. Treatment with dexamethasone was continued, and the patient was discharged home. Three weeks after placement of the ventriculoperitoneal shunt, the patient was admitted again to the other hospital because of streptococcal infection. Two months after discharge, and 10 months after the development of initial symptoms, he was seen in the rheumatology clinic of this hospital for additional evaluation.

That's a pretty common symptom, so I need to narrow it down.
He's in shock, which is a serious condition.
Shock can be due to various reasons like blood loss, infection, or something else.
He also has severe abdominal tenderness and guarding, which makes me think of something like appendicitis because that's a classic presentation with right lower quadrant pain and guarding.
He had one episode of bloody diarrhea.
That's concerning because it could indicate an infection or something like a foodborne illness.
Also, his abdominal pain occurs soon after eating and lasts about 3 hours.
That timing makes me think of something related to digestion, maybe an issue in the small intestine.

Maybe the shock is related to that, but the abdominal symptoms are more concerning for something acute.

The most likely condition is probably appendicitis, but I should consider other possibilities like mesenteric adenoma or maybe a food poisoning.
However, appendicitis is more common in this presentation, especially with the history of recurrent pain after meals.
Wait, but he's in shock.

prompt: A 49-year-old man was admitted to this hospital after being found outdoors in early autumn with obtundation, followed by increasing agitation. On the afternoon of admission, the patient was found leaning up against a wall, unresponsive. With him was a half-filled bottle of cloudy liquid with possible pill fragments, as well as bottles of prescription medications that had been filled earlier that day, including trazodone (1 of 28 pills remaining) and risperidone, buspirone, and loratadine (each with all pills present). Emergency medical services were called. On examination of the patient in the field, the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score was 4 on a scale of 3 to 15 (with lower scores indicating a lower level of consciousness); he opened his eyes in response to painful stimuli but did not move or make any sounds. The blood pressure was 108/67 mm Hg, the pulse 90 beats per minute and regular, the respiratory rate 10 breaths per minute, and the oxygen saturation 97%. The skin was pink, warm, and dry, and the pupils were 3 mm in diameter, round, and reactive to light; the remainder of the examination was reportedly normal. The capillary blood glucose level was 108 mg per deciliter. Oxygen (at a rate of 15 liters per minute, delivered by means of a nonrebreather face mask) and naloxone were administered, without improvement in mental status. An electrocardiogram (ECG) was normal. He was transported to this hospital by ambulance. The patient’s history, which was obtained from his medical records, included drug use (cocaine, opiates, and benzodiazepines), anxiety, depression with multiple suicide attempts, hepatitis C virus infection, and possible chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Current medications other than those found with him on presentation were unknown. He had no known allergies. He smoked cigarettes and had been homeless and incarcerated in the past. He was divorced and had adult children; his current living circumstances were not known. On examination in the emergency department, the patient could move his arms and legs and open his eyes in response to painful stimuli, but he could not follow commands or speak; the GCS score was 8. The blood pressure was 108/67 mm Hg, the pulse 88 beats per minute, the temperature 36.2°C, the respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, and the oxygen saturation 97% while he was breathing ambient air. Both pupils measured 3 mm in diameter and were briskly reactive to 2 mm when exposed to bright light. The lungs were clear with normal respiratory effort, the breath sounds were diminished at the bases, the heart sounds were normal, and the abdomen was soft. Within the first 45 minutes after his arrival at the hospital, the patient became increasingly agitated and combative, resisting all medical interventions; physical restraints were applied. An ECG showed sinus rhythm at a rate of 86 beats per minute, with evidence of biatrial enlargement and with a PR interval of 128 msec, a QRS interval of 104 msec, a QT interval of 386 msec, and a corrected QT (QTc) interval of 461 msec. A complete blood count and blood levels of calcium and phosphorus were normal; other test results are shown inTable 1. Analysis of urine obtained by means of straight catheterization revealed a pH of 5.5 and a specific gravity of 1.008; dipstick testing was normal. Screening of a blood specimen for toxins revealed trazodone (1826 μg per liter; therapeutic range, 800 to 1600), meta-chlorophenylpiperazine (MCPP), and venlafaxine; screening of a urine specimen was negative. The poison control center advised monitoring cardiac intervals with serial ECG. Approximately 4 hours after arrival, a repeat ECG showed a QTc interval of 501 msec. Shortly thereafter, the patient vomited. Magnesium was administered. Laboratory Data. On admission, the patient had intermittent somnolence alternating with periods of increasing agitation and thrashing limbs, but he remained nonverbal and unable to follow commands. Low-dose lorazepam for extreme agitation and normal saline were administered. Increasing lower abdominal fullness developed that was consistent with bladder distention and urinary retention; an indwelling urinary catheter was placed, with improvement. On repeat blood testing 7.5 hours after presentation, blood levels of calcium, phosphorus, total protein, albumin, globulin, and troponin T were normal, as were results of liver-function tests; other test results are shown inTable 1. The blood pressure was 109/64 mm Hg, and the pulse 105 beats per minute; the temperature, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation were normal. Ten hours after presentation, blood levels of calcium, phosphorus, and creatine kinase were normal; additional laboratory test results are shown inTable 1. A diagnostic test was performed.

prompt: A 2-year-old child, fed on milk diet, presents with persistent diarrhea, acidic stools (pH of stools less than 5.5) on two separate occassions and presence of 1% of reducing substances in the fresh stools.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 2-year-old child who's been having persistent diarrhea with acidic stools and some reducing substances.
Let me break this down step by step.
First, the child is on a milk diet.
That makes me think about common issues related to milk consumption.
Diarrhea in young children, especially when they're fed on a milk-based diet, can be linked to various digestive disorders.
The presence of acidic stools (pH less than 5.5) is interesting.
I remember that acidic stools can be a sign of something like gastroenteritis, maybe from a bacterial infection, but I'm not sure if that's the only possibility.
The other thing mentioned is the presence of 1% reducing substances in the fresh stools.
Reducing substances in stools are usually indicative of undigested lactose.

Lactose is a sugar found in dairy products, so if the child isn't properly absorbing it, it can pass through the intestines and be fermented by bacteria, leading to the production of acids, which can cause the stool to be acidic.
This makes me think of lactose intolerance.
Wait, but lactose intolerance in a 2-year-old is possible, especially if they're not getting the right enzymes to break down lactose.
However, I also recall that in young children, especially under a year old, they might not have the enzyme lactase, which is needed to digest lactose.
But this child is 2 years old, so maybe they've been introduced to cow's milk or other dairy products.
Another possibility is that the child has a more severe condition like Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, which are forms of inflammatory bowel disease.

These can cause chronic diarrhea, blood in the stool, and altered stool pH. But the presence of reducing substances in the stool is more commonly associated with lactose issues rather than inflammatory bowel disease.
I should also consider other causes of diarrhea, like infections (e.g., rotavirus, which is common in young children and causes acidic stools), parasites, or food allergies.
However, the presence of reducing substances points more towards lactose not being fully absorbed, which suggests lactose intolerance or a maldigestion issue.
Wait, but in lactose intolerance, the stool can be acidic because the undigested lactose is fermented by bacteria, producing acids.
So the low pH is consistent with that.
The reducing substances (like glucose and galactose) are the result of lactose not being broken down properly.
So putting it all together, the child is on a milk diet, has acidic stools, and shows reducing substances in the stool.
This points towards lactose maldigestion or lactose intolerance.
Since they're on a milk diet, it's likely that they're consuming dairy products, and their body isn't properly absorbing the lactose, leading to the symptoms.
I don't think it's just a simple infection because the presence of reducing substances is a more specific indicator of undigested lactose.
Also, while infections can cause diarrhea, they might not necessarily produce reducing substances in the stool in the same way.
Therefore, the most likely diagnosis here is lactose intolerance or lactose maldigestion.
The child's symptoms of persistent diarrhea with acidic stools and reducing substances in the stool, coupled with a milk diet, strongly suggest lactose intolerance or lactose maldigestion.
The presence of reducing substances indicates undigested lactose, which is typically due to a deficiency in the enzyme lactase, leading to maldigestion or intolerance.

prompt: An 80 year old asymptomatic woman on a routine examination was detected to have a monoclonal spike on serum electrophoresis (IgG levels 1.5 g/dl). Bone marrow revealed plasma cells of 8%.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 80-year-old woman.
She's asymptomatic, but her routine exam showed a monoclonal spike on serum electrophoresis with IgG levels at 1.5 g/dl.
The bone marrow also showed plasma cells at 8%.
Hmm, let's break this down.
Monoclonal spikes in the serum usually indicate a plasma cell disorder.
The IgG level being elevated suggests a problem with immunoglobulins, specifically IgG.
Since she's asymptomatic, it's not something like multiple myeloma which often presents with symptoms like bone pain or kidney issues.
The bone marrow showing plasma cells at 8% is a bit low, but it's still concerning.
In multiple myeloma, plasma cells are usually higher, like 10-20%, but sometimes they can be lower.
Maybe she's early in the course of the disease or it's a different type.
Wait, but she's asymptomatic.
Could it be something else?
Maybe a benign monoclonal gammopathy.
That's when there's a monoclonal protein in the blood without any symptoms.
It's often seen in conditions like monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) or multiple myeloma.
But with the bone marrow showing plasma cells, it's more likely to be multiple myeloma.
Even if the percentage is a bit low, the presence of plasma cells in the bone marrow is a key factor.

Also, the IgG level is elevated, which aligns with multiple myeloma since it's a heavy chain disease affecting IgG.

So, putting it all together, the most likely diagnosis is multiple myeloma.

The asymptomatic nature might just mean she's in an early stage or the disease is just starting, but the lab results point towards multiple myeloma.

prompt: A 41-year-old woman was admitted to this hospital because of decreased visual acuity in the left eye and diplopia. The patient had been well until 7 weeks before admission, when, in late summer, a moderate frontal headache developed on the left side and then completely resolved after several hours. On awakening the next morning, the left side of her face was numb from lower eyelid to mouth and from nose to ear. She was evaluated in the emergency department of another hospital. Computed tomography (CT) of the head, performed without the administration of contrast material, revealed no evidence of hemorrhage, mass, mass effect, or other intracranial abnormalities. The patient was discharged home. During the next 2 weeks, numbness persisted in the middle of the face; evaluations by her primary care provider, a neurologist, and a dentist did not reveal any abnormalities. Two weeks after the onset of symptoms, the numbness resolved, but ptosis of the left upper eyelid developed, along with double vision that was characterized by one image appearing diagonally over the other. The patient presented to a second hospital, where CT and CT angiography of the head and neck revealed mucosal thickening in the ethmoid sinuses and the left sphenoid sinus, as well as air–liquid levels in the maxillary sinuses bilaterally. A complete blood count, white-cell differential count, and metabolic panel were normal, and a pregnancy test was negative. A 2-week course of an unspecified antibiotic agent was administered. Several days later, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head, performed after the administration of gadolinium, reportedly revealed changes consistent with sinusitis but was otherwise normal. Visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes, and an ophthalmologist prescribed an eye patch to treat diplopia. Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid that was obtained during a lumbar puncture (including nucleic acid testing for herpes simplex virus) and blood cultures were reportedly negative. Two weeks before admission, periorbital pain on the medial left side developed, without pressure, headache, or double vision. One week later, diplopia recurred, with associated abnormal deviation of the left eye. Results of studies of visual evoked potential were nondiagnostic. In the left eye, visual acuity was decreased and color discrimination was abnormal. Three days before admission, the patient had nausea and vomiting, along with vertigo that resulted in her falling in her bathroom. Diplopia persisted, and she rated left periorbital pain at 5 on a scale of 0 to 10 (with 10 indicating the most severe pain). The evening before admission, repeat MRI was performed at the second hospital. MRI of the head revealed abnormal soft tissue along the anterior and lateral walls of the left sphenoid sinus, in the left orbital apex, and extending posteriorly into the left cavernous sinus. This soft tissue was intermediate in intensity on both a T2-weighted image (Figure 1A) and a contrast-enhanced T1-weighted image (Figure 1B). A coronal contrast-enhanced MRI image (Figure 1C) showed abnormal enhancement at the junction of the cavernous sinus and Meckel’s cave on the left side, with enhancing tissue extending to the inner aspect of the foramen ovale. Imaging Studies of the Sinuses and Orbits.MRI of the orbit was performed at another hospital. An axial T2-weighted image (Panel A) and an axial contrast-enhanced T1-weighted image (Panel B) show tissue of intermediate intensity lining the sphenoid sinus and involving the left orbital apex and the cavernous sinus (arrows). A coronal contrast-enhanced T1-weighted image (Panel C) shows enhancing soft tissue that extends inferiorly to the foramen ovale. An axial CT image of the orbit (Panel D) shows that the bone between the sphenoid sinus and the orbital apex is relatively intact despite the presence of abnormal soft tissue on both sides (arrow). On the basis of the results of MRI, the patient was advised to go immediately to the emergency department of this hospital. On arrival, she reported that ibuprofen provided minimal relief of periorbital pain. She had no history of fever, night sweats, chest pain, dysuria, diarrhea, rashes, muscle or joint aches, or weight loss. She had hypothyroidism, chronic rhinosinusitis, and environmental allergies to mold and dust; she had had herpes zoster involving the trigeminal nerve that had resolved and had undergone excision of a breast fibroadenoma in the past. Medications included levothyroxine, aspirin, a calcium supplement with vitamin D, and ibuprofen for pain. She had no known allergies to medications. She lived with her husband and children and worked from her home. She drank alcohol occasionally and did not smoke or use illicit drugs. Her maternal grandfather had had lymphoma; other family history was not known. On examination, the temperature was 37.4°C; the other vital signs and oxygen saturation were normal. Ophthalmologic examination revealed visual acuity of 20/20 in the right eye and 20/400 in the left eye. The pupils were equal, round, and reactive, with a left afferent pupillary defect. Results of color-vision testing with Ishihara color plates were normal on the right side (8/8 correctly identified) and 0/8 on the left. Intraocular pressure was 13 mm Hg on the right side and 11 mm Hg on the left. Slit-lamp examination revealed normal anterior segments bilaterally. Examination of extraocular motility revealed full motility in the right eye; the left eye had limited adduction, supraduction, and infraduction and no abduction, with minimal intorsion on attempted abduction (Figure 2). Trace ptosis of the left upper eyelid was present, and margin reflex distances were 4.5 mm in the right eye and 3.5 mm in the left. Levator function was normal, at 15 mm bilaterally. Exophthalmometry measurements were 16 mm in the right eye and 18 mm in the left, with a base of 92 mm. There was mildly reduced sensation in response to pinprick in the second branch of the fifth cranial nerve on the left side, and facial strength was normal. Results of funduscopic examination were unremarkable bilaterally; the optic nerves were normal, without pallor, edema, or hemorrhages. Results of visual-field testing, which was performed reliably on each eye, were normal on the right side; the left side had a large central scotoma, with preservation of the peripheral vision. Endoscopic endonasal examination revealed that the turbinates were moderately hypertrophied; a left septal bone spur and mild-to-moderate septal deviation were present. The remainder of the otolaryngologic, neurologic, and general examinations was normal. Photographs of the Patient’s Eyes.In primary gaze (Panel C), there is mild ptosis of the left upper eyelid. The left eye has mild deficits of elevation (Panel A), adduction (Panel B), and depression (Panel E), and no abduction (Panel D). The hematocrit, hemoglobin level, white-cell count, differential count, platelet count, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were normal, as were blood levels of electrolytes, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, glucose, C-reactive protein, angiotensin-converting enzyme, and immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, and IgM) and results of renal-function and coagulation tests. prompt: 28 year patient from Bihar presents with on and off pain in right scrotum and then gradual onset swelling develops over the duration of 2 years. Trans illumination test is positive. Top of testis can be reached.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 28-year-old patient from Bihar.
He's presenting with on and off pain in the right scrotum and a gradual onset of swelling over two years.
The trans illumination test is positive, and the top of the testis can be reached.
First, I remember that the trans illumination test (TIT) is used to check for a hydrocele.
When you shine a light behind the testis, if the light can be seen through the scrotum, it suggests an inguinal hernia because the hernia allows light to pass through the inguinal canal.
But wait, the patient also has pain and swelling.
So, maybe it's not just a simple hernia.
The gradual onset of swelling makes me think of an inguinal hernia because they usually develop over time.
The pain being on and off could be due to the hernia causing discomfort when the bowel moves, like during certain movements.
But the TIT being positive points towards a hernia, as it's a sign of a patent processus vaginatus or inguinal canal.
I should also consider other possibilities.
Could it be a testicular torsion?
That usually presents with sudden, severe pain, but this patient's pain is more on and off, and there's a gradual swelling.
Testicular torsion is more acute, so maybe not.
What about an orchitis or epididymitis?
Those can cause pain and swelling, but the TIT is more specific for hernias.
Orchitis might not show up on TIT, I think.
Another thought: could it be a femoral hernia?
But those are less common and usually present differently, with pain in the groin or thigh, not just the scrotum.
So, putting it all together, the positive TIT and the gradual swelling with pain point towards an inguinal hernia.
The fact that the top of the testis can be reached suggests that the hernia isn't too large, maybe a small inguinal hernia that's causing some discomfort when the patient moves.
The patient's presentation of on and off pain in the right scrotum along with gradual swelling over two years, combined with a positive trans illumination test, strongly suggests an inguinal hernia.
The TIT being positive indicates a patent processus vaginatus, which is characteristic of an inguinal hernia.
The gradual onset of symptoms and the ability to reach the top of the testis support this diagnosis.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 74-year-old man.
Let's go through the information step by step.
He's a 74-year-old man with severe, steady, mild abdominal pain that starts about 30 minutes after eating.
That makes me think about postprandial symptoms, which are symptoms that occur after eating.
The pain is mild but severe, so it's something that's noticeable but not completely debilitating.
He's lost 12 kg over the past few months because he's avoiding eating.
Weight loss can be a symptom of various conditions, but in this context, it's probably related to his abdominal pain.
He doesn't want to eat because it hurts afterward, so he's losing weight as a result.
His abdominal exam during an asymptomatic interval is normal.
That's interesting because it suggests that when he's not having pain, there's nothing obvious on the outside.
No visible distension, no tenderness, nothing that stands out.
The stool guaiac test is negative, which rules out gastrointestinal bleeding because that test is used to detect blood in the stool.
So, no internal bleeding is present.
The colonoscopy and barium studies are also negative.

A colonoscopy is a comprehensive test that checks for a lot of gastrointestinal issues, and barium studies, like a barium enema or barium swallow, are used to look for obstructions or other structural issues in the digestive system.
Both being negative means that there's probably nothing obstructing the intestines, and no significant inflammation or other issues seen during those tests.
His complete blood count is normal too.
That rules out anemia or infection, which are common causes of abdominal pain.
So, the blood work isn't showing anything concerning.
Putting this all together, the key symptoms are postprandial pain and weight loss.
The lack of findings on imaging and lab work points towards a functional gastrointestinal issue rather than a structural one.
The most common condition that fits this is functional dyspepsia, which is a common cause of stomach pain after eating.
It's characterized by epigastric pain that gets worse after meals, burning, and sometimes belching.
It's often related to a sensitive stomach or a motility disorder in the esophagus or stomach.
Functional dyspepsia can sometimes be triggered by certain foods, and that's why he's losing weight—he's avoiding eating to prevent the pain.
The fact that his symptoms are mild but persistent after meals, and the lack of any structural issues on tests, makes functional dyspepsia the most likely diagnosis.
The patient's symptoms of postprandial pain and weight loss, combined with normal diagnostic findings, point to functional dyspepsia.

A diagnosis of focal motor seizures was made; levetiracetam and glucocorticoids were administered. Approximately 2 months after the onset of symptoms, twitching of the arm and hand became nearly constant and was accompanied by facial twitching; a clinical diagnosis of epilepsia partialis continua was made. Intravenous immune globulin was administered, and the twitching in his face and arm almost completely resolved. Approximately 3 months later, however, the symptoms recurred. During the year before this evaluation, the right arm and the right side of the face began to twitch nearly continuously, with more intense focal clonic activity occurring 2 to 20 times per day; there was associated progressive weakness of the muscles of the right arm (more severe distally than proximally) and the right side of the face, increasing spasticity in the fingers and wrist, and subtle weakness of the right leg. There was no history of loss of consciousness, apnea, cyanosis, or seizure activity involving the left side. MRI studies of the head that were performed between 9 months and 3 months before this evaluation reportedly revealed a T2-weighted hyperintense lesion in the left motor strip involving the adjacent white matter and, in more recent studies, the parietal region, with no clear evidence of atrophy. A brain biopsy was recommended. The family sought a second opinion at this hospital. The patient was born at 36 weeks of gestation after the onset of preterm labor and had normal or advanced developmental milestones (including reading at 3 years of age). He had reactive airway disease and had undergone tonsillectomy, adenoidectomy, and urologic surgery. Medications included levetiracetam (800 mg twice daily), clonazepam (0.5 mg in the morning and 1 mg in the evening), oxcarbazepine (360 mg in the morning and 420 mg in the evening), valproic acid (375 mg twice daily), lipoic acid, vitamin B6, and coenzyme Q10. Immunizations were current. He had no known drug allergies. He consumed a ketogenic diet (a high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet), which helped to control his seizures, and he participated in occupational and physical therapy. He lived with his parents and older sibling, was in second grade, and did well academically. His mother and sibling had attention deficit–hyperactivity disorder, a paternal aunt had bipolar disorder, and other paternal relatives had depression. On examination, the patient was awake, alert, and pleasant. His speech was clear and fluent, with mild dysarthria. He seemed to be intelligent, with good social skills. The pupils and extraocular movements were normal. There was weakness on the right side of the face, the palate was elevated symmetrically, and the tongue protruded along the midline. There was nearly continuous twitching of the right lower facial muscles. Muscle bulk, tone, and strength were normal in the left arm and leg. In the right arm, strength was 4/5 proximally, with little movement of the fingers or wrist and distal-muscle spasticity. Strength in the right leg was 4+/5, with slightly increased reflexes. The gait was mildly hemiparetic. A brain biopsy was recommended, and the family resumed care at the other hospital. prompt: A 55-year-old woman with a history of autoimmune hepatitis was admitted to this hospital because of increasing lethargy, anorexia, and abdominal pain. Approximately 7 years before this admission, the patient received a diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis at another hospital, and she began taking prednisone. During the next 6 years, splenomegaly, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, jaundice, and lethargy occurred, as did recurrent episodes of ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and encephalopathy. A diagnosis of portal hypertension was made, and approximately 6 months before this admission, a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) procedure was performed at another hospital. Approximately 3.5 months before this admission, the patient moved to Massachusetts. The following week, she was seen in the emergency department of this hospital because of intermittent headaches, weakness, dizziness, fatigue, and increasing abdominal and ankle swelling. She also had a history of diabetes mellitus type 2, hypertension, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. Her medications included prednisone, lactulose, omeprazole, rifaximin, neomycin, ursodiol, lisinopril, folate, potassium chloride, and insulin. On examination, the patient's vital signs were normal. Conjunctival injection and icterus, subconjunctival hemorrhages, and 2+ pedal edema were present bilaterally, and the abdomen was soft, without tenderness or guarding; the remainder of the examination was normal. Blood levels of urea nitrogen, globulin, magnesium, amylase, and N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide were normal; other test results are shown inTable 1. Ultrasonography of the abdomen with noninvasive Doppler evaluation of the abdominal vasculature revealed splenomegaly, 19 cm in maximal diameter (normal range, <14 cm), and patency of the TIPS. The patient was advised to continue her medications at home, and referrals to a primary care physician and a hepatologist were made. Laboratory Data. Nine days later, the patient was found unresponsive on the floor at home. On examination by emergency medical services personnel, the capillary blood glucose level ranged from 30 to 39 mg per deciliter (1.7 to 2.2 mmol per liter); a glucose infusion was administered, and her condition improved. She was admitted to this hospital. Her physical and laboratory evaluations and imaging studies had not changed from previous examinations. She was discharged home on the second day. During the next month, testing for antinuclear antibody was positive at 1:40 and 1:160 dilutions, with a speckled pattern, and tests for antibodies to smooth muscle and viral hepatitis A, B, and C were negative. Eight weeks before the current admission, she was readmitted to this hospital because of increasing fatigue and confusion of 1 week's duration; she reportedly had stopped taking many of her medications. On examination, she was oriented only to self. The vital signs were normal, the skin jaundiced, the conjunctivae hyperemic, and the abdomen distended and soft, without tenderness. There was 1+ peripheral edema, and the remainder of the general and neurologic examination, except mental status, was normal. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed nonspecific T-wave abnormalities. The glycated hemoglobin level was normal, testing for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus and parvovirus B19 was negative, and the result of a test for Epstein–Barr virus suggested past infection; other test results are shown inTable 1. Urinalysis revealed 3+ glucose (>1000 mg per deciliter) and 1+ bilirubin, with 20 to 50 white cells, 3 to 5 red cells, few bacteria and squamous cells, and very few transitional cells per high-power field; calcium oxalate and mucin were present. Abdominal ultrasonography did not reveal a substantial amount of ascites. The patient's medications were readministered and her mental status improved. A urine culture grew moderate mixed bacteria, and ciprofloxacin was administered for 3 days. The patient was discharged on the fourth day. On follow-up examination on an outpatient basis, increasing peripheral edema was treated with spironolactone and a short course of furosemide, and the condition improved. Insulin was administered on a sliding scale for glucose levels that were as high as 512 mg per deciliter (28.4 mmol per liter). The thyrotropin level was 6.17 μU per milliliter (reference range, 0.40 to 5.00), and the level of free thyroxine (T4) was normal. Five days before the current admission, the patient returned to this hospital because of confusion, increasing lethargy, nonradiating midabdominal pain, and vomiting. An abdominal ultrasound examination was performed to assess the patency of the TIPS. Transverse images, obtained with and without the use of color-flow Doppler techniques, showed a patent TIPS, with normal velocities and hepatopetal flow in the main portal vein. Splenomegaly was also noted, with the spleen measuring 19.5 cm in maximal diameter. Furosemide was administered intravenously and then orally, and other medications were continued, with symptomatic improvement. Hepatology consultants calculated a Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score of 20 (on a scale of 6 to 40, with higher scores indicating more severe disease), and an outpatient evaluation for liver transplantation was recommended. The blood level of IgA was 561 mg per deciliter (reference range, 69 to 309); blood levels of IgG and IgM were normal, with a normal pattern and without a detectable M component, and a follow-up measurement of blood levels of lactic acid was also normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the liver performed after the intravenous administration of gadolinium revealed marked morphologic features of nodular cirrhosis and signs of portal hypertension, including splenomegaly (19 cm in maximal diameter), upper abdominal varices, and a small amount of ascites. The main portal vein appeared patent, with proper positioning of the TIPS (Figure 1). Abdominal MRI Image.A coronal image from a T2-weighted sequence shows hepatic morphologic features of cirrhosis as well as splenomegaly and a small amount of upper abdominal ascites. The patient was discharged on the fourth day, with the plan that a visiting nurse would follow up. The next day, the patient's anorexia and leg edema were exacerbated, and her oral intake decreased. Constant, ill-defined midabdominal pain occurred, without fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, hematuria, hematochezia, melena, chest pain, dyspnea, lightheadedness, or syncope. She returned to this hospital the following day. The patient's medications included prednisone, lactulose, rifaximin, furosemide, spironolactone, glimepiride, insulin, neomycin, potassium chloride, folic acid, lisinopril, ursodiol, calcium and vitamin D supplements, and omeprazole. She was allergic to intravenous contrast material, which caused angioedema. She was born in Central America, spoke only Spanish, and immigrated to the United States more than 25 years previously. She did not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. There was no family history of liver or other gastrointestinal disease, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or cardiac disease. On examination, the temperature was 37.1°C; the other vital signs and oxygen saturation were normal. The patient had a depressed affect. There were bilateral subconjunctival hemorrhages and diffuse jaundice. The abdomen was soft, with normal bowel sounds and epigastric and mild lower abdominal tenderness during deep palpation and without distention, hepatomegaly, or a palpable spleen. There was no evidence of asterixis, and the remainder of the examination was normal. Laboratory-test results are shown inTable 1. An ECG was unchanged, as compared with the ECG obtained 8 weeks before this admission. The patient was admitted to this hospital. Outpatient medications were continued; ceftriaxone and metronidazole were administered intravenously, and nutritional supplements were provided. On the second day, computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen performed after the oral administration of contrast material revealed cirrhosis with splenomegaly (span, 16.2 cm) and a TIPS in the proper position. In addition, diffuse wall thickening within the cecum and ascending colon, pericolonic fat stranding, and surrounding subcentimeter lymph nodes were present (Figure 2). The differential diagnosis for these findings includes ischemic, infectious, and inflammatory causes, although the right-sidedness is suggestive of neutropenic colitis. Abdominal CT Scan.On the second day, an abdominal CT scan was obtained after the oral administration of contrast material. An axial image through the lower abdomen shows cecal-wall thickening, with surrounding fat stranding and small lymph nodes. Hypotension, to 75/45 mm Hg, developed 2.5 hours after CT was performed. Laboratory-test results are shown inTable 1. Normal saline was infused, albumin and 4 units of red cells were transfused, and antihypertensive agents and diuretics were stopped; there was gradual improvement in blood pressure. Blood specimens were obtained for culture, and vancomycin, linezolid, ciprofloxacin, and cefepime were administered. Later that day, melena occurred. On the fifth day, a diagnostic procedure was performed.
true_dx: Gastric mucormycosis caused by rhizopus species.

prompt: A 50-year-old woman complains of clumsiness in her hands while working in the kitchen: She recently burned her hands on the stove without experiencing any pain. Neurologic examination reveals bilateral weakness of the shoulder girdles, arms, and hands as well as a loss of pain and temperature sensation covering the shoulder and upper limb in a cape-like distribution. Severe atrophy is present in the intrinsic muscles of the hands.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 50-year-old woman.
Let me go through the information step by step.
She's complaining of clumsiness in her hands while working in the kitchen.
That makes me think she's having some kind of motor issue with her hands.
But then she mentions she recently burned her hands on the stove without feeling any pain.
Hmm, that's interesting because usually, when you burn yourself, you'd feel the heat and try to pull away.
The lack of pain suggests something's wrong with her ability to sense pain or temperature in that area.
Looking at the neurological exam: bilateral weakness in the shoulder girdles, arms, and hands.
So both sides are affected.
The weakness is in the upper body, which makes me think of a condition that affects the nerves controlling those muscles.
Also, there's a loss of pain and temperature sensation in the shoulder and upper limb, specifically in a cape-like distribution.
That area is usually covered by the brachial plexus, which is a network of nerves in the neck that controls the skin and muscles in the chest, shoulder, and arm.
The severe atrophy in the intrinsic muscles of the hands also points towards a problem with the nerves responsible for those muscles.
Atrophy usually means the muscles are wasting away, which can happen if the nerves aren't sending the necessary signals to maintain them.
Putting this together, the lack of pain and temperature sensation, along with the distribution of the symptoms, makes me think of a lesion in the brachial plexus.

The direct pupillary reflex is absent, but the indirect (consensual) response is normal.
Wait, the direct reflex is when the eye is stimulated directly, like with a light, and the pupil should constrict.

But the indirect response, which is when you shine a light in one eye and the other pupil constricts, is normal.

That makes me think that the optic nerve itself isn't completely non-functional because the consensual response requires the optic nerve to signal to the brain, so if it were completely dead, the indirect response might also be absent.
So maybe it's not a complete optic nerve lesion.

Edema in the optic disc is often seen in conditions like papilledema, which is swelling of the optic nerve head.

This is common in conditions affecting the optic nerve, such as optic neuritis, which can be caused by demyelinating diseases like multiple sclerosis (MS), or perhaps acute angle-closure glaucoma, though that's more about the angle of the eye, not the optic nerve itself.

A lumbar puncture returns clear, colorless CSF under normal pressure. An electroencephalogram shows diffuse slowing. A CT scan of the brain reveals moderate atrophy.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 76-year-old man.

He's presenting with progressive memory loss and disorientation.
Those are both signs of cognitive issues, probably related to dementia or something similar.
His pupils are small but react normally to light, so that makes me think it's not something affecting the brainstem or causing an abnormal response, like in a comatose state.
His muscle tone is normal, so no signs of rigidity or other neurological issues there.
The lumbar puncture (LP) results show clear, colorless CSF under normal pressure.
Normal CSF can rule out things like bacterial meningitis or something causing an alteration in CSF clarity.
The fact that the pressure is normal might also help differentiate from conditions like hydrocephalus, which can cause increased intracranial pressure.
The EEG shows diffuse slowing.
I remember that diffuse slowing on EEG is often seen in conditions affecting the entire brain, like in a metabolic issue or a degenerative process.
It can also be seen in conditions like diffuse encephalopathy, which is a general term for brain inflammation or dysfunction.
The CT scan shows moderate atrophy.
Atrophy can be seen in various conditions, but the location and extent matter.
Since it's moderate, it's probably not something like severe atrophy from something like Alzheimer's, which often has more pronounced changes, especially in the temporal regions.
But moderate atrophy could be part of the picture in several conditions.
Putting this together, the key symptoms are memory loss and disorientation with normal CSF and EEG showing slowing.
The CT shows atrophy.
So, the most likely diagnosis is probably a form of dementia.
Given the age and the presence of atrophy, it's likely Alzheimer's disease.
But I should consider other possibilities like vascular dementia or maybe even something like frontotemporal dementia, but those often have more specific symptoms and maybe different EEG findings.
The diffuse slowing on the EEG is more in line with Alzheimer's, which typically affects the temporal lobes and causes a characteristic pattern on EEG.
Wait, but the CT shows moderate atrophy.
Alzheimer's does cause atrophy, especially in the hippocampus and temporal lobes.
The diffuse slowing on the EEG supports this.
The normal CSF rules out infections or other causes.
So,
yeah,

The patient's symptoms of progressive memory loss and disorientation, along with the findings from the EEG and CT scan, point towards Alzheimer's disease.
The diffuse slowing on the EEG is characteristic of Alzheimer's, and the moderate atrophy seen on CT aligns with the neurodegenerative changes associated with this condition.
The normal CSF further supports this diagnosis by ruling out infectious or inflammatory causes.

prompt: Ms. Caren T. Harris(Pediatric Surgery): A 9-year-old girl was admitted to this hospital because of loss of consciousness and seizures. The patient had had recent inguinal pain and swelling but had been otherwise well until the morning of admission, in early autumn, when she fell down one stair at home and struck her head. A hematoma developed on the right side of the forehead, without loss of consciousness or other injury. Shortly thereafter, she ate breakfast and then attended a previously scheduled appointment in the outpatient surgery clinic of this hospital to evaluate inguinal pain and swelling on the left side that had lasted for approximately 3 weeks and was near the site of an inguinal herniorrhaphy that had been performed 9 months earlier. On examination, there was mildly tender lymphadenopathy inferior to the left inguinal crease, with a 2-mm punctate lesion superficial to one of the lymph nodes. There were no findings suggestive of cellulitis. Ultrasound studies were scheduled for the next day. Shortly after the patient visited the clinic, approximately 2 hours after she fell down the stair, she fell again from a standing position to the ground at a shopping mall, hitting her head a second time. The patient’s mother reported that the patient was on the ground, moaning, and “frothing at the mouth” and that she had tonic–clonic movements, with both arms flexed and both feet extended. The patient also had urinary incontinence and one episode of vomiting. The movements resolved within 30 to 60 seconds. Emergency medical services were called. On examination, the patient was in a supine position, crying, and drifting in and out of consciousness. The pulse was 120 beats per minute, and the respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. The pupils were sluggishly reactive. The patient had spontaneous movement of all limbs, with posturing movements such as bilateral arm retractions to her chest and foot inversions. Oxygen was administered at a rate of 15 liters per minute through a nonrebreather mask, a cervical collar was applied, and she was placed on a backboard and transported by ambulance to this hospital. During transport, one episode of vomiting occurred. The capillary blood glucose level was 108 mg per deciliter, and cardiac monitoring revealed sinus tachycardia without ectopy. She arrived at the emergency department 40 minutes after the second fall. The history was obtained from the patient’s mother. The patient was born after a full-term gestation, had had normal growth and development, and was right-handed. She had undergone bilateral inguinal herniorrhaphies 9 months earlier. Three weeks before this admission, after returning from a 2-month visit to Puerto Rico, the patient reported discomfort and swelling in the left inguinal region. Her pediatrician prescribed a course of amoxicillin, which she began taking 9 days before this admission; the prescription was changed to amoxicillin–clavulanic acid after 2 days and then stopped 2 days later by the patient’s mother because of lack of improvement and possible facial swelling. The patient had received all routine childhood vaccinations, took no other medications, and had no other known allergies. She was born in Puerto Rico and moved to the United States with her mother at 4 years of age. She lived with her mother, stepfather, and siblings in an urban area and was a student. She returned to Puerto Rico in the summers to visit her father. During the most recent visit, she was exposed to mosquitoes, stray kittens, and a pet dog. Her father had hypertension, and other relatives had asthma; there was no family history of seizures or other neurologic diseases. On examination, the patient had incomprehensible speech, was intermittently moaning, and did not follow commands; she had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 10 on a scale of 3 to 15 (with lower scores indicating a lower level of consciousness). The temperature was 36.4°C, the blood pressure 71/51 mm Hg, the pulse 95 beats per minute, and the respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute; the oxygen saturation ranged from 97% to 100% while she was breathing ambient air. There was a hematoma (2.5 cm by 2.5 cm) on the forehead and facial abrasions on the right side. The pupils were round, equal, and sluggishly reactive to light, decreasing from 4 mm to 3 mm in diameter. The patient opened her eyes and had spontaneous movement of her arms and legs, with intermittent diffuse posturing movements. On passive movement, there was more rigidity on the right side than on the left. The left inguinal area contained two palpable lymph nodes (5 mm in diameter) and a 2-mm punctate lesion superficial to one of the lymph nodes, without overlying warmth, erythema, or fluctuance. The remainder of the examination was normal. The white-cell count was 14,000 per cubic millimeter (reference range, 4500 to 13,500), the blood level of potassium was 3.2 mmol per liter (reference range, 3.4 to 4.8), the phosphorus level was 3.5 mg per deciliter (reference range, 4.5 to 5.5), and the glucose level was 134 mg per deciliter (reference range, 70 to 110). The hematocrit, hemoglobin level, white-cell differential count, platelet count, and anion gap were normal, as were blood levels of other electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, amylase, and lipase and results of renal- and liver-function tests. Screening of the blood for toxins was negative. An electrocardiogram revealed sinus tachycardia at a rate of 134 beats per minute. Diazepam was administered, and the posturing movements transiently resolved; the blood pressure increased to 125/84 mm Hg. Computed tomography (CT) of the cervical spine and head was performed. CT of the cervical spine, performed with a cervical collar in place, revealed straightening of the normal cervical lordosis and no acute osseous injury. CT of the head revealed a small subgaleal hematoma adjacent to the right frontal bone, without evidence of an underlying fracture. There was no evidence of acute intracranial hemorrhage. A small arachnoid cyst was seen in the right middle cranial fossa. Ms. Harris:Approximately 40 minutes after arrival, the patient became less responsive and posturing movements were present. The blood pressure was 119/88 mm Hg, and the respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute; the oxygen saturation decreased to 84% while she was breathing ambient air. On examination without the cervical collar, the neck was supple. Vomitus was suctioned from the airway, and high-flow oxygen was administered. Etomidate and rocuronium bromide were administered intravenously, and the trachea was intubated for airway protection. The patient was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit. Three hours after arrival in the emergency department, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head was performed. MRI of the head revealed restricted diffusion involving the cortex of the right temporal lobe, right occipital lobe, right superior and inferior parietal lobule, and right cingulate gyrus, as well as the right insula and right thalamus (Figure 1A and 1B); fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images showed hyperintense signal and mild mass effect related to gyral swelling. Given the patient’s recent seizure activity, these findings are consistent with excitotoxicity. In a patient with seizure activity, signal abnormality and contrast enhancement due to disruption of the blood–brain barrier can be observed on MRI and are typically transient. In this case, T1-weighted images that were obtained after the administration of contrast material showed no abnormal enhancement (Figure 1C). Three-dimensional time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography of the intracranial circulation revealed increased flow-related enhancement of the right middle cerebral artery, the right posterior cerebral artery, and their branches (Figure 1D) that was due to marked hyperemia on the side of the epileptic focus. Findings associated with hyperemia can also be observed on perfusion imaging. Because seizure-related MRI findings are usually transient, follow-up imaging can be helpful to differentiate abnormalities due to seizures from those due to other causes. MRI and Magnetic Resonance Angiography of the Head.MRI of the head was performed on admission. An axial diffusion-weighted image (Panel A) and apparent-diffusion-coefficient map (Panel B) show restricted diffusion of the right insula (thin arrow), the right thalamus (arrowhead), and the cortex of the right temporal lobe (thick arrow) and right occipital lobe, with associated mild gyral swelling. An axial T1-weighted image (Panel C), obtained after the administration of contrast material, shows no abnormal enhancement. Mild swelling of the right frontal soft tissues, which is related to the patient’s recent falls, was noted incidentally. A maximum-intensity-projection image (Panel D) was obtained from three-dimensional time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography of the intracranial circulation. The image shows increased flow-related enhancement of the right middle cerebral artery (arrow), the right posterior cerebral artery (arrowhead), and their branches, as compared with the contralateral arteries; in a patient with seizure activity, these findings are consistent with hyperemia. The MRI findings could be explained by the patient’s recent seizure activity, but the differential diagnosis for these findings also includes MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes), an inherited disorder of intracellular energy production that causes seizures and strokelike cortical lesions that cross vascular territories. Although the findings on imaging, including the pattern of involvement and the absence of contrast enhancement, argue against an infectious cause, infectious causes should also be considered. Ms. Harris:Levetiracetam was administered. Electroencephalography (EEG) followed by 24-hour EEG monitoring revealed continuous generalized background slowing in the delta and theta ranges, frequent intermittent focal delta-range slowing over the right hemisphere (with maximal slowing at times over the right anterior quadrant or right temporal region), and frequent sharp waves in the right frontotemporal region. Seven hours after the patient’s arrival, lumbar puncture was performed. Analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed clear, colorless fluid, with a glucose level of 92 mg per deciliter (reference range, 50 to 75) and a total protein level of 33 mg per deciliter (reference range, 5 to 55), as well as 5 red cells per cubic millimeter and no white cells, other nucleated cells, or xanthochromia. Gram’s staining revealed very few neutrophils and mononuclear cells and no organisms. Cultures of the blood, urine, and CSF were obtained. Management decisions were made, and additional diagnostic tests were performed.

prompt: A 25 - years old married infeile woman having regular menstruation, fever, lower abdominal pain and dysmenorrhoea present herself at the OPD. On examination, there are bilateral soft tender masses of 3cm diameter in both fornices and uterus is of normal size.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 25-year-old woman.
She's married, has regular menstruations, but she's presenting with fever, lower abdominal pain, and dysmenorrhea.
On examination, there are bilateral soft tender masses in both fornices, and the uterus is of normal size.
First, I'll consider her age.
She's 25, so she's in the reproductive age group, which makes gynecological issues more likely.
She has regular periods, so her menstrual history isn't pointing me towards something like anovulation or PCOS immediately.
She's complaining of fever and lower abdominal pain.
Fever could be a sign of an infection, maybe an abscess or something like endometritis.
The dysmenorrhea suggests menstrual-related pain, which could be due to inflammation or another issue.
The physical exam findings are key here.
Bilateral soft tender masses in the fornices.
Fornices are the areas on either side of the uterus where the fallopian tubes open into the peritoneal cavity.
Soft masses there could indicate something like a tubo-ovarian abscess, which is an infection in the fallopian tubes or ovaries.
These abscesses can cause fever, pain, and dysmenorrhea because the infection can spread and cause inflammation.
The uterus is of normal size, so that makes me think it's not something like a large fibroid or something that would cause the uterus to enlarge.
Also, since the masses are in the fornices, it's more likely related to the fallopian tubes or ovaries rather than the uterus itself.
I should also consider other possibilities.
Could it be something like appendicitis?
But appendicitis usually presents with more right lower quadrant pain and less so in the fornices.
Ovarian torsion is another thought, but that usually presents with sudden severe pain and maybe some signs of shock, which I don't see mentioned here.
Another possibility is endometritis, which is an infection of the uterus lining.
That can cause fever and pain, but the masses in the fornices are more specific to the fallopian tubes or ovaries, so maybe it's a tubo-ovarian abscess.
So putting it all together, the fever, pain, and the masses in the fornices point towards a tubo-ovarian abscess.
This is an infection that can occur after a gynecological procedure or from a sexually transmitted infection, given her age and possible sexual activity.
The treatment would likely involve antibiotics and possibly drainage if it's abscessed.
The patient's presentation of fever, lower abdominal pain, and dysmenorrhea along with bilateral soft tender masses in the fornices suggests a tubo-ovarian abscess.
This is an infection involving the fallopian tubes or ovaries, often following an infection or procedure.

He has a daily headache that occurs two times a day for the past three weeks.

That makes me think it's something that happens during sleep because most headaches that wake someone up are often related to sleep disorders.
He mentions tearing and reddening of his right eye, along with nasal stuffiness.
Tearing and redness in one eye could point towards sinusitis because sinus infections can cause those symptoms.
Nasal stuffiness also aligns with sinus issues.
But wait, the pain is deep and excruciating, localized to the right side of his head.
That makes me think it's not just a typical sinus headache but something more specific.
The neurologic examination is nonfocal, so there's no evidence of a stroke or brain lesion.
That rules out some of the more serious neurological issues.
Putting this together, the symptoms seem to fit cluster headaches.
Cluster headaches are known to occur in clusters, often several times a day, and can be very severe.
They typically affect one side of the head and are often accompanied by tearing and redness in the eye on the affected side.
The timing of the headaches waking him up from sleep also matches cluster headaches, as they often occur during sleep.
I don't think it's a migraine because those usually don't have the tearing and redness, and they can be more widespread.
Sinus headaches can cause similar symptoms, but cluster headaches are more specific with the intense pain and the eye symptoms.
Also, cluster headaches are known to be very severe and short in duration, which matches the description.

So, considering all these points, the most likely diagnosis is cluster headache.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 60-year-old woman with a 3-week history of severe headaches.

She's otherwise healthy, which is important because it narrows down the possibilities.
The key clue here is the CT scan result: a small, circular, hypodense lesion with a ring-like contrast enhancement.
First, I remember that on CT scans, contrast enhancement can help differentiate between different types of lesions.
A hypodense lesion means it's darker than the surrounding brain tissue, so it's probably a cyst or something non-enhancing.
But the ring-like enhancement suggests that there's some vascularity or blood-brain barrier breakdown, which makes me think of a hemorrhagic lesion.
I recall that intracranial hemorrhage, especially spontaneous, can present with sudden headaches.
Since she's been having headaches for three weeks, it's possible it's been gradual, but the timing could also be after a minor injury or if she's on blood thinners.
The CT scan showing a small, circular lesion supports this because hematomas or hemorrhages often have a rounded shape.
Another thought is about other possibilities like brain tumors, but tumors are usually more irregular and might show more extensive enhancement.
Meningiomas can be circular but are usually solid, not ring-enhancing.
Cerebral abscesses can cause ring enhancement too, but they're more likely to be larger and may have surrounding edema, which isn't mentioned here.
Given her age and the fact that she's otherwise healthy, the most likely explanation is a spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage.
The ring enhancement on contrast CT is consistent with this diagnosis.

I should also consider if there's any history of trauma or bleeding disorders, but since it's not provided, I'll go with the most common cause for a hypodense, ring-enhancing lesion in a healthy individual.

prompt: A 52-year-old woman was seen in the pulmonary clinic of this hospital for evaluation of a unilateral pleural effusion that had been seen on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the breasts.
